fuentes/carta-de-balboa-1513/titulo.texto: Letter from Vasco Núñez de Balboa to the King (January 20, 1513)

fuentes/carta-de-balboa-1513/escrita.lug.texto: Santa María la Antigua del Darién

fuentes/carta-de-balboa-1513/resumen.texto: Report that Balboa sent to the king from Santa María la Antigua del Darién, months before crossing the isthmus. It describes the chiefdoms of the region, their gold, and Indigenous reports of another sea and of rich lands to the south; it asks for reinforcements and criticizes his rivals Enciso and Nicuesa.

fuentes/carta-de-balboa-1513/por_que_imp.texto: It is the first report by a governor of the isthmus and the origin of the exploration of the Pacific and of Peru.

fuentes/carta-de-zumarraga-1529/titulo.texto: Letter from Fray Juan de Zumárraga to Charles V (August 27, 1529)

fuentes/carta-de-zumarraga-1529/resumen.texto: A long letter in which the bishop-elect of Mexico denounces the abuses of the first Audiencia (Nuño de Guzmán and the judges, or oidores, Matienzo and Delgadillo): excessive tribute, enslavement and sale of Indians to the islands, use of carriers, violence against Indigenous lords, and the blocking of the letters that were to reach the king. It contributed to the Crown's replacement of that Audiencia.

fuentes/carta-de-zumarraga-1529/por_que_.texto: It is one of the first documents denouncing the mistreatment of Indigenous people in Mexico, written by an ecclesiastical authority.

fuentes/historia-de-los-indios-motolinia.texto: History of the Indians of New Spain

A Franciscan chronicle of the Nahuas before and after the conquest, finished around 1541 and dedicated to the Count of Benavente. It describes festivals, the calendar, and pre-Hispanic sacrifices; the “ten plagues” that fell on the Indians after 1519 (smallpox, war, hunger, tribute, slavery, work in the mines and in the rebuilding of Mexico); and Franciscan evangelization with its mass baptisms. It remained in manuscript for almost three centuries; the reference edition is that of Joaquín García Icazbalceta (1858).
It is a direct testimony of the first years, recording both the violence of the pre-Hispanic world and that of the conquest, written by a Franciscan who defended his missionary method.

fuentes/carta-de-motolinia-a-carlos-v/ti.texto: Letter from Fray Toribio de Motolinía to Emperor Charles V (January 2, 1555)

fuentes/carta-de-motolinia-a-carlos-v/re.texto: A letter written in Tlaxcala in which Motolinía attacks Bartolomé de las Casas: he accuses him of exaggerating figures and facts, of knowing little about the Indians and their languages, of denying absolution to encomenderos, and of discrediting the Spanish before the world. He maintains that the preaching of the Gospel justified Spanish rule and asks the emperor to extend it, although he acknowledges abuses by the conquistadors.

fuentes/carta-de-motolinia-a-carlos-v/po.texto: It is the earliest and best-known criticism of Las Casas from within the Church, written by someone who had also denounced the evils of the conquest; it is cited in the debate over the reliability of A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies.

fuentes/informacion-en-derecho-quiroga/r.texto: A legal brief that Vasco de Quiroga, a judge (oidor) of the Audiencia of Mexico, addressed in 1535 to the Council of the Indies against the royal provision of 1534, which had again allowed the enslavement of Indians taken in war or bought from other Indians as slaves (“de rescate”). He argues that those enslavements were unjust and that pre-Hispanic Indigenous slavery was very different from Castilian slavery; he describes the abuses it caused and proposes gathering the Indians into orderly towns.

fuentes/informacion-en-derecho-quiroga/p.texto: It is one of the strongest legal arguments against Indigenous slavery of its time and the basis of Quiroga's hospital-towns.

fuentes/ordenanzas-de-los-hospitales-de-.texto: Rules and Ordinances for the Government of the Hospitals of Santa Fe de México and Michoacán

Rules that Quiroga left for his hospital-towns: common goods, a common six-hour workday, rotating shifts in the fields, apprenticeship in trades, offices chosen among the families, and care of the sick and of travelers. They are known from late copies, such as the one published by Juan José Moreno in 1766, and their exact date is disputed.
It shows the attempt to apply to Indigenous peoples a model inspired by Thomas More's Utopia, which partly survived in the Purépecha memory of “Tata Vasco.”

fuentes/breve-y-mas-compendiosa-doctrina.texto: A Brief and More Compendious Christian Doctrine in the Mexican and Castilian Languages

A bilingual catechism that, according to references from its time and from later bibliographers, was the first book printed by Juan Pablos in Mexico, in 1539. No copy is known: the oldest surviving items from that press are fragments of the Manual de adultos (1540), an account of the Guatemala earthquake (1541), and Zumárraga's doctrines of 1543 and 1544.
It marks the beginning of printing in America, which in its first decades worked mainly for evangelization in Indigenous languages.

fuentes/arte-de-la-lengua-mexicana-olmos.texto: Grammar for Learning the Mexican Language

The first grammar of Nahuatl, completed by Olmos in 1547 in Hueytlalpan, with examples of traditional speeches (huehuetlatolli). It circulated in manuscript copies and was printed only in 1875, in Paris, in the edition of Rémi Siméon.
It opened the tradition of grammars of American Indigenous languages, the basis of missionary work and today of historical linguistics.
Rémi Siméon edition (Paris, 1875) on Internet Archive

fuentes/codice-de-la-cruz-badiano/titulo.texto: Libellus de medicinalibus Indorum herbis (Cruz-Badiano Codex)

fuentes/codice-de-la-cruz-badiano/resume.texto: An illustrated herbal compiled in 1552 at the College of Santa Cruz in Tlatelolco by the Nahua physician Martín de la Cruz and translated into Latin by Juan Badiano. It describes, with color paintings, more than a hundred plants and their medicinal uses according to Nahua medicine. It was sent to Spain as a gift for Charles V, passed to the Vatican Library, and Pope John Paul II returned it to Mexico in 1990.

fuentes/codice-de-la-cruz-badiano/por_qu.texto: It is the first treatise on American medicine and botany written by Indigenous authors, and it shows both the Latin education of the college and Nahua medical knowledge.

fuentes/vocabulario-de-molina/titulo.texto: Vocabulary in the Castilian and Mexican Languages

fuentes/vocabulario-de-molina/resumen.texto: A Spanish–Nahuatl dictionary printed by Juan Pablos in 1555 and reissued in 1571 by Antonio de Spinosa, enlarged and with a second part in Nahuatl–Spanish. It records the vocabulary of central Mexican Nahuatl in the first decades after the conquest, including the new terms for what came from Europe.

fuentes/vocabulario-de-molina/por_que_im.texto: It is the first dictionary printed in America and the main tool for reading colonial documents in Nahuatl.

fuentes/vocabulario-de-molina/leer.0.tit.texto: Original 1555 edition (Newberry Library) on Internet Archive

fuentes/codice-kingsborough/titulo.texto: Kingsborough Codex (Memorial of the Indians of Tepetlaoztoc)

fuentes/codice-kingsborough/resumen.texto: A memorial with paintings and glosses that the Indigenous people of Tepetlaoztoc, near Texcoco, presented around 1554–1556 to denounce before the Crown the excessive tribute and the mistreatment by their encomenderos since 1522. It depicts, year by year, the goods and services delivered and the violence suffered by the town's lords.

fuentes/codice-kingsborough/por_que_impo.texto: It is one of the most detailed Indigenous testimonies of the weight of early encomienda, presented through the courts.

fuentes/codice-osuna/autor.texto: Indigenous government of Mexico-Tenochtitlan and Tlatelolco

fuentes/codice-osuna/idioma_original.texto: Pictographic with Nahuatl and Spanish glosses

fuentes/codice-osuna/resumen.texto: Paintings with Nahuatl and Castilian glosses presented in 1565 by the Indigenous rulers of Mexico-Tenochtitlan and Tlatelolco during the inspection of Jerónimo de Valderrama. They record labor, materials, and food delivered without payment to officials of Viceroy Luis de Velasco and to judges (oidores) of the Audiencia, in order to demand payment for them.

fuentes/codice-osuna/por_que_importa.texto: It shows Indigenous cabildos using colonial justice and their own pictographic records to denounce abuses by authorities.

fuentes/lienzo-de-quauhquechollan/resume.texto: A large painted cloth made around 1530 by the Nahuas of Quauhquechollan (today Huaquechula, Puebla). It recounts, with a map, their participation as allies of the Spaniards in the conquest of Guatemala, including their route, their battles and their alliance with Jorge de Alvarado. It is kept in Puebla; in 2007 the Universidad Francisco Marroquín of Guatemala published its digital restoration.

fuentes/lienzo-de-quauhquechollan/por_qu.texto: It tells the conquest of Guatemala from the viewpoint of Indigenous allies who claimed merit and privileges: it shows that it was also a war of some peoples against others.

fuentes/lienzo-de-quauhquechollan/leer.0.texto: Digital restoration by the Universidad Francisco Marroquín

fuentes/relaciones-de-pedro-de-alvarado/.texto: Letters from Pedro de Alvarado to Hernán Cortés (1524)

Two letters, from April and July 1524, in which Alvarado informs Cortés of his advance through Soconusco and Guatemala: the battles against the K’iche’, the burning of their lords in Q’umarkaj (Utatlán), the alliance with the Kaqchikels and the war against the Pipil of Cuzcatlán.
It is the testimony of the conquistador himself, written to display his merits, and it acknowledges acts such as the burning of the K’iche’ rulers.

fuentes/informacion-de-1556-guadalupe/ti.texto: Inquiry of 1556 into the sermon of Friar Francisco de Bustamante

fuentes/informacion-de-1556-guadalupe/re.texto: An inquiry ordered by Archbishop Montúfar in September 1556, after the Franciscan provincial Francisco de Bustamante preached against devotion to the image of Guadalupe of Tepeyac, which he considered a risk of idolatry for the Indians and attributed to an Indigenous painter named Marcos. The witnesses describe a growing cult and alms, but none mentions apparitions or Juan Diego. It was published at the end of the 19th century.

fuentes/informacion-de-1556-guadalupe/po.texto: It is the oldest document on the Guadalupe cult: some read it as proof that the account of the apparitions is later, and others as evidence of a cult already established in 1556.

fuentes/relaciones-geograficas/autor.texto: Questionnaire by Juan López de Velasco and responses from corregidores and towns

fuentes/relaciones-geograficas/resumen.texto: Answers to a questionnaire of 50 questions that the Crown sent in 1577 to all the towns of the Indies, on geography, population, languages, ancient history, government, wars, crops and resources. From New Spain more than a hundred relaciones survive, along with dozens of maps painted by Indigenous artists, which blend Mesoamerican and European conventions.

fuentes/relaciones-geograficas/por_que_i.texto: It is the most complete description of 16th-century New Spain, with Indigenous testimony on tribute, war and the population decline after the conquest.

fuentes/historia-eclesiastica-indiana/re.texto: A history of the Franciscan evangelization of Mexico, completed around 1596, which covers pre-Hispanic religion, the arrival of the twelve friars and the work of the first missionaries. Mendieta presents the early years as an ideal Indigenous church and attributes its decline to epidemics, forced labor repartimiento, Spanish greed and Crown policy. García Icazbalceta published it in 1870.

fuentes/historia-eclesiastica-indiana/po.texto: It is the main source for the Franciscan view, which is millenarian and critical of colonial exploitation; Torquemada made extensive use of it.

fuentes/monarquia-indiana/resumen.texto: A history of the peoples of Mexico (origins, government, religion, sacrifices and customs), of their conquest and of their evangelization, printed in Seville in 1615. Torquemada used papers by Olmos, Sahagún and Mendieta and Indigenous annals, sometimes without citing them.

fuentes/monarquia-indiana/por_que_import.texto: For two centuries it was the most widely read history of ancient Mexico, and it preserves data from lost sources.

fuentes/monarquia-indiana/leer.0.titulo.texto: Madrid edition (1723), volume I, on Internet Archive

fuentes/historia-general-remesal/titulo.texto: General History of the West Indies and Particular History of the Government of Chiapa and Guatemala

fuentes/historia-general-remesal/resumen.texto: A chronicle of the Dominican province of San Vicente de Chiapa and Guatemala, published in Madrid in 1619. It recounts the arrival of the Dominicans, the work of Las Casas as bishop of Chiapa, the peaceful conversion of Tezulutlán (Verapaz) and the conflicts with the encomenderos, based on documents from the order.

fuentes/historia-general-remesal/por_que.texto: It is the main source on Verapaz and on Las Casas in Central America, written in defense of the Dominican order.

fuentes/imagen-de-la-virgen-maria-sanche.texto: Image of the Virgin Mary, Mother of God of Guadalupe

The first printed account of the Virgin’s apparitions to Juan Diego in 1531 and of the image on his tilma, read through Revelation chapter 12 as a sign of Mexico’s election. Sánchez cites no earlier documents and says he relies on tradition.
It inaugurated the Guadalupan literature and the Creole patriotism associated with the image.

fuentes/nican-mopohua/resumen.texto: A book in Nahuatl published in 1649 by Luis Lasso de la Vega, vicar of the Guadalupe shrine. Its central part, which begins with the words “Nican mopohua” (“here it is told”), narrates the apparitions to Juan Diego in December 1531. From the late 17th century (Sigüenza y Góngora) the account has been attributed to Antonio Valeriano, written around 1556. Sousa, Poole and Lockhart (1998) argue that Lasso de la Vega himself composed it based on Sánchez’s book, and the question remains disputed.

fuentes/nican-mopohua/por_que_importa.texto: It is the founding text of the Guadalupan cult, central to Mexican identity; its date and authorship are at the center of the historical debate about the apparitions.

fuentes/tratado-de-las-virtudes-del-indi.texto: Treatise on the Virtues of the Indian

A memorial addressed to Philip IV in which Palafox, bishop of Puebla, lists the virtues of the Indians (patience, obedience, detachment, generosity, skill in crafts) and asks that they be protected from the abuses of corregidores, doctrineros and hacendados.
It shows a defense of Indigenous peoples from the ecclesiastical hierarchy in the mid-17th century, with the paternalistic outlook of the era.

fuentes/libra-astronomica/resumen.texto: A treatise written in 1681 and published in 1690, in which Sigüenza defends his Manifiesto filosófico against comets and refutes the Exposición astronómica of Eusebio Kino, who saw in the comet of 1680 an omen of misfortune. He argues, with observations and calculations, that comets are natural phenomena, and cites Copernicus, Galileo, Kepler and Descartes with the caution that censorship imposed.

fuentes/libra-astronomica/por_que_import.texto: It is one of the first defenses in the Americas of the modern scientific method against astrology.

fuentes/recordacion-florida/autor.texto: Francisco Antonio de Fuentes y Guzmán

fuentes/recordacion-florida/resumen.texto: A history of the Kingdom of Guatemala written around 1690 by a Creole regidor of Santiago, a descendant of Bernal Díaz. It describes the conquest, the cities, towns and products of the kingdom, and uses Indigenous titles and paintings that are now lost; it defends the conquistadors and the Creoles and minimizes abuses.

fuentes/recordacion-florida/por_que_impo.texto: It is the main Creole history of Central America, and it preserves information from Indigenous documents that have disappeared.

fuentes/respuesta-a-sor-filotea/titulo.texto: Response of the Poetess to the Most Illustrious Sor Filotea de la Cruz

fuentes/respuesta-a-sor-filotea/resumen.texto: A letter dated March 1, 1691, in which Sor Juana replies to the bishop of Puebla, Manuel Fernández de Santa Cruz, who, under the pseudonym Sor Filotea, had published without her permission the critique she had written of a sermon by the Jesuit António Vieira (the Carta atenagórica, 1690), and advised her to give up secular letters. Sor Juana recounts her life of study and defends, with biblical and classical examples, the right of women to learn and to teach.

fuentes/respuesta-a-sor-filotea/por_que_.texto: It is one of the first American arguments for women’s education and the main autobiographical source on Sor Juana.

fuentes/respuesta-a-sor-filotea/leer.1.t.texto: Fama y obras póstumas (Madrid, 1700), first edition, on Internet Archive

fuentes/primero-sueno/resumen.texto: A silva of 975 lines, published in Seville in 1692, which describes the soul’s attempt, during sleep, to know the whole universe, and its failure. It is Sor Juana’s most ambitious poem, in the manner of Góngora, with references to the science and philosophy of her time.

fuentes/primero-sueno/por_que_importa.texto: It is a peak of Baroque poetry in the Spanish language written in the Americas.

fuentes/gazeta-de-mexico/autor.texto: Juan Ignacio María de Castorena y Ursúa

fuentes/gazeta-de-mexico/resumen.texto: The first newspaper of New Spain, which Juan Ignacio María de Castorena published monthly from January 1722 for six issues, with religious, official and commercial news and reports of ship arrivals. Juan Francisco Sahagún de Arévalo took it up again between 1728 and 1742, and Manuel Antonio Valdés published another Gazeta from 1784.

fuentes/gazeta-de-mexico/por_que_importa.texto: It began periodical journalism in New Spain.

fuentes/escudo-de-armas-de-mexico/resume.texto: A chronicle of the matlazáhuatl epidemic of 1736-1738 in Mexico City, and of the 1737 oath that made the Virgin of Guadalupe patroness of the city to stop it. It gathers the measures taken by the authorities, the rogations and news of the deaths, above all among Indigenous people.

fuentes/escudo-de-armas-de-mexico/por_qu.texto: It is the main source on that epidemic and on the consolidation of the Guadalupan cult in the 18th century.

fuentes/historia-antigua-de-mexico-clavi.texto: A history of the peoples of the Valley of Mexico up to the conquest, published in Italian in Cesena (1780-1781) by an exiled Creole Jesuit. It uses codices, chronicles and his knowledge of Nahuatl; it describes the Mexica sacrifices without concealing them, and closes with dissertations that refute De Pauw, Buffon and Robertson on the supposed inferiority of American nature and inhabitants.
It was the most influential American response in the “dispute of the New World” and a basis of Mexican Creole patriotism.
Original Italian edition (Cesena, 1780) on Internet Archive

fuentes/rusticatio-mexicana/resumen.texto: A poem in Latin hexameters published in Modena (1781) and expanded in Bologna (1782), in which the exiled Guatemalan Jesuit describes lakes, volcanoes, cochineal, indigo, sugar, silver mining, cattle, birds and the games of Mexico and Guatemala.

fuentes/rusticatio-mexicana/por_que_impo.texto: It is the major work of colonial Latin literature and a poetic inventory of the nature and economy of New Spain.

fuentes/ordenanza-de-intendentes-1786/ti.texto: Royal Ordinance for the Establishment and Instruction of Army and Provincial Intendants in the Kingdom of New Spain

fuentes/ordenanza-de-intendentes-1786/re.texto: An ordinance of December 4, 1786 that divided New Spain into twelve intendancies, governed by intendants with powers of justice, treasury, war and policing. It replaced the alcaldes mayores with subdelegados and prohibited the forced distribution of goods to Indians, although the practice partly continued.

fuentes/ordenanza-de-intendentes-1786/po.texto: It is the central administrative reform of the Bourbon reforms in Mexico, prepared by José de Gálvez.

fuentes/real-orden-de-la-expedicion-de-l.texto: Royal Order and Instructions of the Royal Philanthropic Vaccine Expedition

Provisions of 1803 by which the Crown created and financed Francisco Javier de Balmis’s expedition to bring the smallpox vaccine to its American and Asian dominions, with foundling children who kept the vaccine alive arm to arm. They ordered viceroys, governors and bishops to support it, to house the children and to create vaccine boards that would preserve the fluid.
It is the founding document of the first vaccination campaign of worldwide reach.

fuentes/bando-de-hidalgo-1810/titulo.texto: Decree of Miguel Hidalgo against slavery, tribute and stamped paper

fuentes/bando-de-hidalgo-1810/resumen.texto: An edict issued in Guadalajara on December 6, 1810, which orders slaveholders to free their slaves within ten days, under penalty of death, abolishes the tribute paid by Indians and castes, and eliminates the use of stamped paper. It restated an earlier edict by the insurgent José María Anzorena in Valladolid (October 1810).

fuentes/bando-de-hidalgo-1810/por_que_im.texto: It is one of the first proclamations of the abolition of slavery in Spanish America, although the war limited its effect.

fuentes/sentimientos-de-la-nacion/resume.texto: A document of 23 points that Morelos read on September 14, 1813, when he installed the Congress of Chilpancingo. It proclaims the independence of America, the Catholic religion as the only one, popular sovereignty, the separation of powers, the abolition of slavery and of caste distinctions, the suppression of tribute and torture, and laws that “moderate opulence and indigence.”

fuentes/sentimientos-de-la-nacion/por_qu.texto: It is the political program of the insurgency and one of the founding texts of Mexican constitutionalism.

fuentes/acta-de-independencia-de-america.texto: Solemn Act of the Declaration of Independence of North America

A declaration of the insurgent congress meeting in Chilpancingo, dated November 6, 1813, which proclaims the dependence on the Spanish throne broken forever. It was the first formal declaration of Mexican independence, with no immediate effect because of Morelos’s defeats.
It is the direct antecedent of the 1821 act and the first sovereign document of the insurgency.

fuentes/constitucion-de-apatzingan/titul.texto: Constitutional Decree for the Liberty of Mexican America

fuentes/constitucion-de-apatzingan/resum.texto: A constitution sanctioned by the insurgent congress in Apatzingán on October 22, 1814. It establishes popular sovereignty, the Catholic religion as the only one, the separation of powers with an executive of three persons, and the rights to equality, security, property and liberty. It never took effect, because the insurgents did not control the territory.

fuentes/constitucion-de-apatzingan/por_q.texto: It is the first written constitution of Mexico.

fuentes/plan-de-iguala/resumen.texto: A proclamation signed by Iturbide on February 24, 1821, which proposes the independence of New Spain as a constitutional monarchy, offered to Ferdinand VII or to a prince of his house, with three guarantees: the Catholic religion as the only one, independence, and union between Americans and Europeans. It declares all inhabitants citizens without distinction of origin and creates the Army of the Three Guarantees, which Guerrero and most of the royalist chiefs joined.

fuentes/plan-de-iguala/por_que_importa.texto: It was the pact between royalists and insurgents that made Mexican independence possible within a few months.

fuentes/tratados-de-cordoba/resumen.texto: An agreement signed on August 24, 1821 by Iturbide and the political chief Juan O’Donojú in Córdoba (Veracruz), which recognizes the independence of the Mexican Empire according to the Plan of Iguala and leaves open the choice of monarch should the Bourbons not accept. The Spanish Cortes declared it null in 1822; Spain recognized Mexican independence in 1836.

fuentes/tratados-de-cordoba/por_que_impo.texto: It gave legal cover to the entry of the Army of the Three Guarantees into Mexico and to the formation of the Empire.

fuentes/acta-de-independencia-del-imperi.texto: Act of Independence of the Mexican Empire

An act signed on September 28, 1821 by the Provisional Governing Junta, one day after the entry of the Army of the Three Guarantees into Mexico City, which declares the Mexican nation sovereign and independent of old Spain. It was signed by Iturbide, O’Donojú and the other members of the junta.
It is the birth certificate of the independent Mexican state.

fuentes/acta-de-independencia-de-centroa.texto: Act of Independence of Central America

An act approved on September 15, 1821 in Guatemala City by a junta of authorities, the archbishop, the town council and residents, which declares independence “to prevent the consequences that would be dreadful if the same people proclaimed it on their own.” Drafted by José Cecilio del Valle, it kept Gabino Gaínza as political chief and left the form of government to a congress that never met before the annexation to Mexico.
It is the founding document of the Central American republics; its own text says the junta declared independence in order to get ahead of a popular proclamation.

fuentes/constitucion-de-centroamerica-18.texto: Constitution of the Federal Republic of Central America
National Constituent Assembly of Central America

A constitution sanctioned on November 22, 1824, which organizes the federation of Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua and Costa Rica, with a federal president and congress and states with their own governments. It declares all inhabitants free and prohibits the slave trade, confirming the abolition decreed in April 1824.
It is the legal basis of the only political union of Central America after the colonial period.

fuentes/ensayo-politico-nueva-espana/tit.texto: Political Essay on the Kingdom of New Spain

fuentes/ensayo-politico-nueva-espana/res.texto: A study published in Paris between 1808 and 1811, based on Humboldt’s stay in 1803-1804 and on the censuses, reports and viceregal archives that the authorities opened to him. It analyzes geography, the population by castes, agriculture, silver mining, trade and finances; it praises the Seminario de Minería and Creole science, and describes Mexico as a country of inequality, with an impoverished Indigenous majority subject to tribute.

fuentes/ensayo-politico-nueva-espana/por.texto: It was the most complete description of New Spain at the end of the colonial period, widely read by independence leaders and by foreign investors in the 19th century.

fuentes/ensayo-politico-nueva-espana/lee.texto: English translation by John Black (London, 1811) on Internet Archive

fuentes/relacion-del-espantable-terremot.texto: Account of the Dreadful Earthquake That Has Now Happened Again in the Indies in a City Called Guatimala

An account signed by the notary Juan Rodríguez about the destruction of Santiago de Guatemala by the flood of water and mud from the Volcán de Agua in September 1541, in which the governor Beatriz de la Cueva and many residents died. As its title says, it is presented as an example so that readers may amend their sins. It was printed in Mexico in 1541 at the workshop of Juan Pablos and is also known from a Spanish reprint of the same century.
It is one of the oldest surviving prints from the Mexican press, and it is considered the first news publication of the Americas.
Spanish reprint of the 1541 Mexican edition (Boston Public Library) on Internet Archive

fuentes/carta-de-icazbalceta-sobre-guada.texto: Letter on the Origin of the Image of Our Lady of Guadalupe of Mexico

A confidential letter that the historian Joaquín García Icazbalceta wrote in 1883, at the request of the archbishop of Mexico, on the historical evidence for the Guadalupe apparitions. It concludes that no 16th-century document mentions them, starting with the writings of Zumárraga. It was published in 1896, after his death and without his permission, and caused a scandal.
It is the first documented critical analysis of the Guadalupan tradition, made by a Catholic and the greatest Mexican bibliographer of the 19th century.

fuentes/la-conquista-espiritual-de-mexic.texto: A thesis on the methods of the Franciscans, Dominicans and Augustinians in New Spain between 1523 and 1572: language learning, catechisms, colleges, new towns, and missionary art and theater. Ricard concludes that the evangelization created a church without an Indigenous clergy, which he considers its great failure.
It is the classic work on the evangelization of Mexico; later historiography, such as Lockhart’s, criticized it for looking only from the friars’ side and not from Indigenous communities.

fuentes/soldiers-indians-and-silver/resu.texto: A history of the war between the Spaniards, with their Indigenous allies, and the Chichimec peoples along the silver road from Zacatecas: attacks on convoys, presidios, enslavement of captives, and the final “peace by purchase,” with food and clothing deliveries and Tlaxcalan colonists.

fuentes/soldiers-indians-and-silver/por_.texto: It is the classic study of that war; its author later argued, in Tree of Hate (1971), that the Black Legend was propaganda against Spain.

fuentes/aztecs-under-spanish-rule/resume.texto: A study of the Indigenous peoples of the Valley of Mexico during the colonial period, based on archives: encomienda, repartimiento, tribute, land, haciendas, cabildos, the Church and the population decline. Gibson documents the exploitation and also the persistence of communities and of their forms of government.

fuentes/aztecs-under-spanish-rule/por_qu.texto: It is a reference work on Indigenous life under Spanish rule, which went beyond a history written only from the conquistadors’ and friars’ perspective.

fuentes/spanish-central-america-macleod/.texto: Socioeconomic History of Spanish Central America, 1520-1720

An economic history of the Audiencia of Guatemala that follows its export cycles (Indigenous slaves, cacao, indigo) and their relation to the decline of the Indigenous population, forced labor and the depression of the 17th century.
It is the leading synthesis on early colonial Central America.

fuentes/forced-native-labor-sherman/titu.texto: Forced Indigenous Labor in 16th-Century Central America

fuentes/forced-native-labor-sherman/resu.texto: A documentary study of Indigenous slavery, the encomienda, the cargadores (tamemes) and personal service in the Audiencia of Guatemala, including the export of slaves from Nicaragua and Honduras to Panama and Peru, and the application of the New Laws by Alonso López de Cerrato.

fuentes/forced-native-labor-sherman/por_.texto: It is the reference work on forced labor and the trade in Indigenous people in Central America.

fuentes/justice-by-insurance/titulo.texto: The General Indian Court in New Spain

fuentes/justice-by-insurance/resumen.texto: A study of the General Indian Court, the tribunal that from the late 16th century handled Indigenous lawsuits quickly and cheaply, financed by a tax of half a real per tributary. Borah reconstructs its background, its procedure and its wide use by Indigenous individuals and communities, including against caciques, Spaniards and other towns.

fuentes/justice-by-insurance/por_que_imp.texto: It is the reference study on special justice for Indigenous people in New Spain.

fuentes/conquest-and-survival-lovell/tit.texto: Conquest and Cultural Change: The Cuchumatanes Highlands of Guatemala, 1500-1821

fuentes/conquest-and-survival-lovell/res.texto: A historical geography of the Maya peoples of the Cuchumatanes from the conquest to independence: demographic collapse from epidemics, congregations, tribute and loss of land, and the survival of communities that kept their languages and territory.

fuentes/conquest-and-survival-lovell/por.texto: It is a key regional study of the impact of colonization on the Maya of Guatemala.

fuentes/indian-survival-nicaragua-newson.texto: A study of the Indigenous population of Nicaragua since the conquest: wars, the export of slaves to Panama and Peru, epidemics and forced labor, which reduced it drastically in the 16th century, and the very different survival of the peoples of the Pacific and of those of the Caribbean.
It is the main demographic reconstruction of colonial Nicaragua.

fuentes/nahuas-after-the-conquest/resume.texto: A social history of the Nahuas of central Mexico based on documents the Nahuas wrote themselves in Nahuatl: wills, cabildo minutes, lawsuits and annals. Lockhart shows that the altépetl, the nobility and many pre-Hispanic institutions survived, adapted, within the pueblos de indios, through stages of linguistic and cultural change.

fuentes/nahuas-after-the-conquest/por_qu.texto: It renewed the study of the colonial period by reading it from Indigenous sources.

fuentes/our-lady-of-guadalupe-poole/titu.texto: Our Lady of Guadalupe: Origins and Sources of a Mexican National Symbol, 1531-1797

fuentes/our-lady-of-guadalupe-poole/resu.texto: A review of the sources on the Guadalupe apparitions. Poole, a Vincentian priest, concludes that there is no testimony to them before 1648 and that the devotion was mainly Creole until the 18th century; defenders of the historicity counter with oral tradition and documents such as the Códice Escalada, whose authenticity is itself disputed.

fuentes/our-lady-of-guadalupe-poole/por_.texto: It is the main modern critical work on the origin of the Guadalupan account.

fuentes/megadrought-and-megadeath/autor.texto: Rodolfo Acuña-Soto, David W. Stahle, Malcolm K. Cleaveland and Matthew D. Therrell

fuentes/megadrought-and-megadeath/soport.texto: Scientific article (Emerging Infectious Diseases, vol. 8, no. 4)

fuentes/megadrought-and-megadeath/resume.texto: An article that attributes the cocoliztli epidemics of 1545 and 1576 to a hemorrhagic fever, possibly transmitted by rodents and native to the region, favored by the worst drought in 500 years, reconstructed from tree rings. It estimates between 5 and 15 million deaths in 1545 and about 2 million in 1576, figures that depend on high estimates of the earlier population.

fuentes/megadrought-and-megadeath/por_qu.texto: It is the basis of the hypothesis of an American pathogen behind the 16th-century epidemics, later debated by ancient DNA studies.

fuentes/megadrought-and-megadeath/leer.0.texto: Article in Emerging Infectious Diseases (open access)

fuentes/salmonella-teposcolula/titulo.texto: Genomes of Salmonella enterica from Victims of a Major 16th-Century Epidemic in Mexico

fuentes/salmonella-teposcolula/autor.texto: Åshild J. Vågene, Alexander Herbig, Johannes Krause and others

fuentes/salmonella-teposcolula/resumen.texto: A study of ancient DNA from individuals buried in the cemetery of Teposcolula-Yucundaa (Oaxaca) during the epidemic of 1545-1550, which found in ten of them genomes of Salmonella enterica Paratyphi C, the cause of an enteric fever. The authors propose it as a probable cause of the cocoliztli, without ruling out other pathogens that the method does not detect; a study from the same year found this bacterium in Norway around the year 1200, which supports its arrival from Europe.

fuentes/salmonella-teposcolula/por_que_i.texto: It is the first direct genetic evidence of a pathogen from a colonial epidemic in the Americas.

fuentes/asian-slaves-seijas/resumen.texto: A study of the enslaved people from Asia (called “chinos,” although they came mostly from the Philippines, India and Southeast Asia) brought to Mexico by the Manila galleon, and of their lawsuits for freedom, until the Crown equated them with the Indian vassals and ordered their liberation in 1672.

fuentes/asian-slaves-seijas/por_que_impo.texto: It revealed a little-known trade and the use of Indies law by the enslaved people themselves.

fuentes/empire-of-law/titulo.texto: Empire of Law and Indigenous Justice in Colonial Mexico

fuentes/empire-of-law/resumen.texto: A study of how the Indigenous people of New Spain used the colonial courts in the 16th and 17th centuries to defend land, freedom and rights against Spaniards, caciques and other communities. Owensby argues that the king’s justice was a real tool for Indigenous people and a basis of the legitimacy of the colonial order, without this eliminating abuses.

fuentes/empire-of-law/por_que_importa.texto: It is a reference in the debate on the role of Indies law in the lives of Indigenous peoples.

personas/antonio-de-mendoza/resumen.texto: First viceroy of New Spain (1535-1550) and afterward of Peru (1551-1552). He organized the viceregal government, supported the printing press, the Colegio de Tlatelolco and the request for a university, personally heard complaints from Indigenous people, and led, with thousands of Indigenous allies, the campaign of the Mixtón War (1541-1542), in which prisoners were enslaved. The visita of Francisco Tello de Sandoval accused him of having had prisoners killed with cannons and dogs in that war; he was acquitted.

personas/luis-de-velasco/resumen.texto: Second viceroy of New Spain (1550-1564). He applied the New Laws, freeing enslaved Indigenous people; promoted the first congregations of towns and the Hospital Real de Naturales; opened the university in 1553; and organized Legazpi’s expedition to the Philippines. The Códice Osuna records Indigenous complaints about unpaid work for his officials.

personas/martin-enriquez-de-almanza/resu.texto: Fourth viceroy of New Spain (1568-1580) and afterward of Peru. He expelled John Hawkins’s fleet from San Juan de Ulúa (1568), received the Inquisition tribunal (1571), faced the cocoliztli epidemic of 1576, and hardened the Chichimec War with presidios and the enslavement of captives.

personas/pedro-moya-de-contreras/resumen.texto: First inquisitor of New Spain (1571), later archbishop of Mexico and interim viceroy (1584-1585). He presided over the Third Provincial Council of Mexico (1585) and a general visita that removed and punished officials for corruption.

personas/revillagigedo/nombre.texto: Juan Vicente de Güemes, Count of Revillagigedo

personas/revillagigedo/resumen.texto: Viceroy of New Spain from 1789 to 1794. He ordered the first general census of the viceroyalty (1790-1793) and the paving, lighting and cleaning of the capital, and supported the Seminario de Minería and the Botanical Expedition.

personas/juan-de-zumarraga/resumen.texto: A Basque Franciscan, first bishop (1528) and first archbishop of Mexico (1546-1548), with the title of protector of the Indians: in 1529 he denounced the abuses of the first Audiencia and promoted the printing press, the Colegio de Tlatelolco and the Hospital del Amor de Dios. In a letter of 1531 he said he had destroyed 500 temples and 20,000 idols, and as inquisitor he had Don Carlos Ometochtzin burned in 1539. The accusation that he burned the archives of Texcoco, spread in the 19th century, has no document from his time, as García Icazbalceta noted (1881).

personas/motolinia/resumen.texto: One of the twelve Franciscans who arrived in Mexico in 1524; he adopted the Nahuatl nickname Motolinía (“the poor one”). He wrote the Historia de los indios de la Nueva España, which describes both the pre-Hispanic sacrifices and the “ten plagues” that the conquest brought, and in 1555 a letter to Charles V against Las Casas, whom he accused of exaggeration. He defended mass baptisms and rapid evangelization.

personas/pedro-de-gante/resumen.texto: A Flemish Franciscan, said to be a relative of Charles V, who arrived in 1523, before the twelve. Around 1527 he founded the school of San José de los Naturales, where he taught reading, writing, music and trades to thousands of Indigenous children, and in 1553 he published a Christian doctrine in Nahuatl. He was a lay brother his whole life.

personas/andres-de-olmos/resumen.texto: A Franciscan who arrived in Mexico in 1528 with Zumárraga, with whom he had worked in witchcraft trials in Biscay. He completed the first grammar of Nahuatl in 1547, collected the huehuetlatolli (speeches of the elders), and did missionary work among the Totonacs and Huastecs until his death in Tampico.

personas/alonso-de-molina/resumen.texto: A Franciscan who came to Mexico as a child and learned Nahuatl by playing with Indigenous children. His Vocabulario (1555, expanded in 1571) was the first printed dictionary in the Americas and remains the basis for reading classical Nahuatl; he also wrote confessionals and a grammar (1571).

personas/jeronimo-de-mendieta/resumen.texto: A Basque Franciscan who arrived in 1554 and finished the Historia eclesiástica indiana around 1596. He saw in the early years of evangelization an ideal Indigenous church, and criticized the forced distribution of labor and the mistreatment of Indians; his work remained unpublished until 1870.

personas/juan-de-torquemada/resumen.texto: A Franciscan, guardian of the convent of Tlatelolco and author of the Monarquía indiana (Seville, 1615), the most complete history of its time on the peoples of Mexico, their conquest and their evangelization. He used papers by Olmos, Sahagún and Mendieta and Indigenous sources, sometimes without citing them.

personas/juan-pablos/resumen.texto: A printer from Lombardy (Giovanni Paoli) sent by the Sevillian Juan Cromberger, who in 1539 set up the first documented printing press in the Americas, in Mexico City. He printed at least 35 books: doctrines in Spanish and Indigenous languages, works by Zumárraga and Alonso de la Veracruz, and Molina’s Vocabulario (1555).

personas/martin-de-la-cruz/resumen.texto: A Nahua physician linked to the Colegio de Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco, author in 1552 of the herbal known as the Codex De la Cruz-Badiano, which Juan Badiano translated into Latin. Very little is known about his life.

personas/juan-badiano/resumen.texto: A Nahua from Xochimilco, student and teacher at the Colegio de Tlatelolco, who in 1552 translated into Latin the herbal of Martín de la Cruz. He is an example of Indigenous people trained in Latin and the humanities at the Franciscan college.

personas/antonio-valeriano/resumen.texto: A Nahua from Azcapotzalco trained at the Colegio de Tlatelolco, a collaborator of Sahagún and Indigenous governor of Mexico-Tenochtitlan from 1573 to 1599. Since the late 17th century he has been credited with the Nican mopohua, an attribution that several historians (Sousa, Poole and Lockhart, among others) dispute.

personas/carlos-ometochtzin/resumen.texto: A Nahua lord of Texcoco, son of Nezahualpilli, baptized and educated by the Franciscans. Accused of keeping idols and of urging the nobles to return to the ancient religion, he was tried by Zumárraga’s episcopal Inquisition and burned in Mexico City in November 1539; the punishment was criticized from Spain, and the case weighed on the exclusion of Indians from the Inquisition.

personas/alonso-de-montufar/resumen.texto: A Dominican from Granada, second archbishop of Mexico (1551-1572). He presided over the provincial councils of 1555 and 1565, promoted devotion to the image of Guadalupe of Tepeyac, and for this reason in 1556 confronted the Franciscan provincial Francisco de Bustamante, who considered it a danger of idolatry.

personas/vasco-de-quiroga/resumen.texto: A Castilian jurist, oidor of the second Audiencia of Mexico (1531) and first bishop of Michoacán. He founded the hospital-towns of Santa Fe de México (1532) and La Laguna (1533), inspired by Thomas More’s Utopia, and the Colegio de San Nicolás in Pátzcuaro, and in 1535 he wrote against the enslavement of Indians. The Purépechas remember him as “Tata Vasco”; he also had long land disputes with encomenderos and towns.

personas/juan-de-palafox/muerte.lugar.texto: El Burgo de Osma-Ciudad de Osma

personas/juan-de-palafox/resumen.texto: Bishop of Puebla (1640-1655), visitor and interim viceroy (1642). He donated his library to form the Biblioteca Palafoxiana (1646), wrote a memorial on the virtues of the Indians asking that they be protected, and clashed with the Jesuits over tithes and parishes; he was beatified in 2011.

personas/francisco-hernandez-de-toledo/r.texto: Physician to Philip II, who sent him as protomédico to New Spain (1571-1577) to study its plants and animals, in what is considered the first scientific expedition to the Americas. With Indigenous physicians, informants and painters he described some 3,000 plants; his manuscripts burned in El Escorial in 1671 and are known through printed summaries published in Mexico (1615) and Rome (1651).

personas/bartolome-de-medina/resumen.texto: A merchant from Seville who in 1554, in Pachuca, perfected the patio process, the amalgamation of silver with mercury. The method multiplied silver production in Mexico and Peru and exposed workers to mercury poisoning.

personas/andres-de-urdaneta/resumen.texto: A sailor from Gipuzkoa and Augustinian friar who in 1565 found the return route from the Philippines to Mexico across the North Pacific (the tornaviaje), which made the Manila galleon possible for 250 years.

personas/enrico-martinez/resumen.texto: A cosmographer and printer of German origin (Heinrich Martin) who from 1607 directed the drainage of the Valley of Mexico through Huehuetoca, dug with the forced labor of thousands of Indigenous people. He was blamed for the great flood of 1629; he also wrote the Repertorio de los tiempos (1606).

personas/miguel-sanchez-bachiller/resume.texto: A Creole priest who published in 1648 Imagen de la Virgen María, Madre de Dios de Guadalupe, the first printed account of the Tepeyac apparitions, which he interpreted as a sign of God’s election of Mexico.

personas/luis-lasso-de-la-vega/resumen.texto: Vicar of the Guadalupe hermitage who published in 1649, in Nahuatl, the Huei tlamahuiçoltica, whose central part is the account of the apparitions known as the Nican mopohua.

personas/juan-diego/resumen.texto: An Indigenous man to whom, according to the Nican mopohua (1649), the Virgin of Guadalupe appeared at Tepeyac in 1531. He does not appear in documents of accepted authenticity dated before 1648 (the Códice Escalada, dated 1548 and known since 1995, is disputed); his historical existence was questioned in 1996 by the abbot of the basilica, Guillermo Schulenburg, and the Catholic Church canonized him in 2002.

personas/servando-teresa-de-mier/resumen.texto: A Dominican from Monterrey who in a sermon of 1794 argued that the image of Guadalupe was on the cloak of Saint Thomas the Apostle, preacher of the Americas, and was exiled to Spain. He escaped from several prisons, wrote in favor of independence, and was a constituent deputy for Mexico in 1824.

personas/sor-juana-ines-de-la-cruz/nacim.texto: Nepantla de Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz

personas/sor-juana-ines-de-la-cruz/resum.texto: A Jeronymite nun, the greatest writer of colonial America: poetry, theater, villancicos (some with parts in Nahuatl) and the Primero sueño. In the Respuesta a sor Filotea (1691) she defended women’s right to study; shortly afterward she gave up letters and handed over her library, in circumstances that historians interpret in different ways. She died in 1695 during an epidemic in her convent.

personas/carlos-de-siguenza-y-gongora/re.texto: A Creole scholar, professor of mathematics at the University of Mexico and royal cosmographer. In the Libra astronómica (1690) he argued against Kino that comets are not omens; he gathered codices and Indigenous papers inherited from the Alva Ixtlilxóchitl family, and in the 1692 riot he saved documents from the fire at the palace, a riot he described with contempt for Indians and castes.

personas/eusebio-kino/resumen.texto: A Jesuit from Tyrol who from 1687 did missionary work in the Pimería Alta (Sonora and Arizona), where he founded some twenty missions and introduced cattle and wheat. His journeys and maps showed that California was not an island; in Mexico he published in 1681 an Exposición astronómica on the comet of 1680, which Sigüenza refuted.

personas/jose-antonio-alzate/resumen.texto: A Creole priest and naturalist, editor of scientific newspapers such as the Gacetas de literatura de México (1788-1795). He wrote about cochineal, astronomy and natural history, and defended Indigenous practical knowledge against Linnaeus’s classification.

personas/francisco-javier-clavijero/resu.texto: A Creole Jesuit from Veracruz, expelled with his order in 1767. In exile in Bologna he wrote the Storia antica del Messico (1780-1781), which defended the peoples and nature of America against De Pauw, Buffon and Robertson and became a basis of Mexican Creole patriotism.

personas/rafael-landivar/nacimiento.luga.texto: Santiago de los Caballeros de Guatemala

personas/rafael-landivar/resumen.texto: A Guatemalan Jesuit, expelled in 1767, who in exile in Bologna wrote in Latin the Rusticatio Mexicana (1781-1782), a poem on the nature, crafts and peoples of Mexico and Guatemala.

personas/martin-sesse/resumen.texto: An Aragonese physician who directed the Royal Botanical Expedition to New Spain (1787-1803) and the Botanical Garden of Mexico. With Mociño and Mexican illustrators he described thousands of plants, but the work remained unpublished until the late 19th century.

personas/jose-mariano-mocino/resumen.texto: A Creole physician and naturalist from Temascaltepec, a member of the Botanical Expedition, with which he traveled from Nootka (Canada) to Guatemala. He wrote Noticias de Nutka (1793), about the peoples of that island, and emigrated to Spain in 1803.

personas/fausto-elhuyar/resumen.texto: A chemist from La Rioja who isolated tungsten with his brother Juan José (1783). From 1788 he directed mining in New Spain and the Real Seminario de Minería (1792), the first technical mining school in the Americas.

personas/andres-manuel-del-rio/resumen.texto: A mineralogist from Madrid, professor at the Seminario de Minería in Mexico. In 1801 he discovered in an ore from Zimapán a new element that he called erythronium; a French analysis classed it as chromium, and in 1830 Sefström rediscovered it as vanadium.

personas/francisco-javier-de-balmis/resu.texto: A physician from Alicante at the court who directed the Royal Philanthropic Vaccine Expedition (1803-1806), which took the smallpox vaccine to America and the Philippines, passing it arm to arm through orphan children. Earlier he had lived in New Spain, where he studied plant remedies for venereal diseases.

personas/isabel-zendal/resumen.texto: The director of the orphanage of A Coruña who traveled on Balmis’s expedition caring for the children who carried the vaccine, among them her own son. She settled in Puebla.

personas/alexander-von-humboldt/resumen.texto: A Prussian naturalist who traveled through Spanish America between 1799 and 1804 with the Crown’s permission and spent a year in New Spain (1803-1804). His Ensayo político sobre el reino de la Nueva España (1808-1811) described its population, mining, wealth and inequality, and praised its scientific institutions.

personas/jacinto-canek/resumen.texto: A Yucatec Maya (Jacinto Uc de los Santos) educated by the Franciscans who in November 1761 led a rebellion in Cisteil and had himself crowned king under the name Canek. Defeated within a few days, he was executed in Mérida on December 14, 1761 in a public torture, and his body was burned.

personas/miguel-hidalgo/resumen.texto: A Creole priest of Dolores, former rector of the Colegio de San Nicolás, who began the insurrection on September 16, 1810. In Guadalajara he decreed the abolition of slavery and of tribute (December 1810), and he also ordered the execution of hundreds of Spanish prisoners. Defeated at Puente de Calderón, he was captured, tried and executed by firing squad in Chihuahua in 1811.

personas/ignacio-allende/resumen.texto: A Creole militia captain from San Miguel, organizer of the Querétaro conspiracy and military leader of the 1810 insurgency. He clashed with Hidalgo over the looting and killings by the insurgent crowd; he was executed by firing squad in Chihuahua in 1811.

personas/jose-maria-morelos/resumen.texto: A priest from Michoacán who led the southern insurgency from 1810. He convened the Congress of Chilpancingo, for which he wrote the Sentimientos de la Nación (1813), and that congress issued the Constitution of Apatzingán (1814). Captured in 1815, he was stripped of his orders by the Inquisition and executed by firing squad in San Cristóbal Ecatepec.

personas/felix-maria-calleja/resumen.texto: A royalist military leader who defeated Hidalgo at Aculco and at Puente de Calderón and was viceroy from 1813 to 1816. His repression included mass executions in Guanajuato (1810) and the siege of Cuautla against Morelos (1812).

personas/vicente-guerrero/resumen.texto: A southern insurgent leader of African and Indigenous descent, who kept up guerrilla warfare after Morelos’s death. He agreed with Iturbide to the Plan of Iguala (1821); as president of Mexico he abolished slavery in 1829 and was executed by firing squad in 1831.

personas/agustin-de-iturbide/resumen.texto: A Creole royalist officer who fought the insurgents and in 1821 proclaimed the Plan of Iguala, which united royalists and insurgents and achieved independence. He was emperor of Mexico (1822-1823); he abdicated, went into exile, and was executed by firing squad on his return in 1824.

personas/juan-o-donoju/resumen.texto: A liberal Spanish military officer, the last superior political chief sent to New Spain. On arriving in 1821 he signed with Iturbide the Treaties of Córdoba, which recognized independence, and he died weeks later in Mexico; the Spanish Cortes disowned what he had signed.

personas/vasco-nunez-de-balboa/activo.lu.texto: Santa María la Antigua del Darién

personas/vasco-nunez-de-balboa/resumen.texto: A conquistador from Extremadura who in 1510 helped found Santa María la Antigua del Darién and governed it. In 1513 he crossed the isthmus with Indigenous guides and porters and was the first European to see the Pacific Ocean; on that march, according to Pedro Mártir, he defeated the cacique Cuarecuá and had about forty Indigenous men accused of sodomy thrown to dogs. Pedrarias had him tried and beheaded at Acla in 1519.

personas/pedrarias-davila/resumen.texto: Governor of Castilla del Oro (1514-1526), at the head of the first large expedition organized by the Crown on the mainland, which introduced the Requerimiento. He founded Panama (1519), had Balboa and Francisco Hernández de Córdoba executed, and governed Nicaragua from 1527 until his death; his captains carried out raids of plunder and enslavement that Oviedo and Las Casas denounced.

personas/gil-gonzalez-davila/resumen.texto: A captain who in 1522-1523 traveled along the Pacific coast of Nicaragua, spoke with the cacique the chronicles call Nicarao, and was attacked by the warriors of Diriangén. He reported having baptized tens of thousands of Indigenous people, a figure that cannot be verified, and in 1524 he disputed Honduras with Cristóbal de Olid.

personas/francisco-hernandez-de-cordoba-.texto: A captain sent by Pedrarias Dávila who in 1524 founded Granada and León, in Nicaragua. When he tried to become independent of Pedrarias, he was tried and beheaded in León in 1526.

personas/beatriz-de-la-cueva/resumen.texto: The widow of Pedro de Alvarado, who had herself named governor of Guatemala in September 1541 on learning of her husband’s death: she was the first woman to govern a Spanish province in the Americas. She died days later, when a flood of water and mud from the Volcán de Agua buried the city of Santiago.

personas/francisco-marroquin/resumen.texto: The first bishop of Guatemala (consecrated in 1537). He founded schools and the Santiago hospital, published a doctrine in K’iche’ (1556), and left funds for a college that gave rise to the Universidad de San Carlos.

personas/alonso-lopez-de-cerrato/resumen.texto: A jurist who presided over the Audiencia of Guatemala from 1548 to 1555 and applied the New Laws strictly: he freed thousands of enslaved Indigenous people, prohibited carrying them like beasts of burden, and set new tribute rates. The encomenderos accused him of favoring his relatives; Las Casas praised him.

personas/antonio-de-remesal/resumen.texto: A Galician Dominican who lived in Guatemala and Chiapas and in 1619 published a history of the Dominican province of Chiapa and Guatemala, the main source on Las Casas in Central America and on Verapaz, written from the Dominican order’s perspective.

personas/lempira/resumen.texto: A Lenca chief who in 1537 led, from the peñol of Cerquín (Honduras), an alliance of peoples against the forces of Francisco de Montejo. The sources differ on his death: Antonio de Herrera says a gunshot killed him during a peace conversation, while the probanza of the soldier Rodrigo Ruiz (1558) says he was killed in combat. He is a national hero of Honduras and gives his name to its currency.

personas/francisco-antonio-de-fuentes-y-.texto: Francisco Antonio de Fuentes y Guzmán

A Guatemalan Creole, a descendant of Bernal Díaz del Castillo, regidor of Santiago de Guatemala and author of the Recordación florida (around 1690), a history of the Kingdom of Guatemala that defends the conquistadors and the Creoles and uses Indigenous titles now lost.

personas/pedro-de-betancur/nombre.texto: Pedro de San José de Betancur

personas/pedro-de-betancur/resumen.texto: A Franciscan tertiary from Tenerife who in Santiago de Guatemala founded a hospital for poor convalescents and a primary school; after his death his brotherhood gave rise to the Bethlehemite order, which spread through the Americas. He was canonized in 2002.

personas/pablo-presbere/resumen.texto: Chief of Suinse, in Talamanca (Costa Rica), who led the 1709 uprising against the Franciscan missionaries and the Spaniards, in which friars and soldiers died and fourteen churches were burned. Captured, he was executed by firing squad in Cartago in 1710; Talamanca remained outside Spanish control for the rest of the colonial period.

personas/william-paterson/resumen.texto: A Scottish merchant and co-founder of the Bank of England (1694), who promoted the Scottish colony of Darien (1698-1700). He traveled with the first expedition and survived its failure, in which his wife and son died.

personas/jose-cecilio-del-valle/resumen.texto: A Honduran lawyer who drafted the Act of Independence of Central America (1821). He was a deputy in Mexico and a minister of Iturbide, and a figure of the Federal Republic; he died shortly after being elected its president.

personas/gabino-gainza/resumen.texto: A Spanish military officer, the last captain general of Guatemala, who accepted independence on September 15, 1821 and remained as political chief. He promoted the annexation to Iturbide’s Empire (January 1822).

personas/jose-matias-delgado/resumen.texto: A priest from San Salvador who took part in the 1811 movement against the Spanish authorities and signed the 1821 act. He led Salvadoran resistance to annexation by Mexico and presided over the constituent assembly of the Federal Republic (1823-1824).

personas/robert-ricard/resumen.texto: A French historian, author of La conquista espiritual de México (1933), the classic study of the evangelization by the mendicant orders between 1523 and 1572.

hechos/fundacion-de-santa-maria-la-antig.texto: Founding of Santa María la Antigua del Darién
Santa María la Antigua del Darién

The first stable Spanish city on the American mainland, founded in 1510 by Martín Fernández de Enciso and Vasco Núñez de Balboa in Darién (today Colombia), after defeating the cacique Cémaco and occupying his town. It was the seat of the first bishopric on the continent (1513) and the capital of Castilla del Oro until Pedrarias moved the government to Panama; it was abandoned in 1524.

hechos/balboa-llega-al-mar-del-sur/resum.texto: In September 1513 Vasco Núñez de Balboa crossed the Isthmus of Panama with about 190 Spaniards and hundreds of Indigenous guides and porters. On September 25 he saw from a ridge the ocean he called the South Sea, and days later he took possession of it in the Gulf of San Miguel. Along the way, according to Pedro Mártir de Anglería, he defeated the cacique Cuarecuá, who died with hundreds of his men, and had about forty Indigenous men accused of sodomy thrown to dogs.

hechos/castilla-del-oro-de-pedrarias/tit.texto: Governorship of Castilla del Oro of Pedrarias Dávila

hechos/castilla-del-oro-de-pedrarias/res.texto: The expedition of Pedrarias Dávila, of some 1,500 people, reached Darién in 1514 as the first large enterprise organized by the Crown on the mainland, with the Requerimiento as the legal instrument of the conquest. Hundreds of settlers soon died of hunger and disease, and the raids of his captains plundered and enslaved the chiefdoms of the isthmus, as denounced by Oviedo, who served as the colony’s veedor, and by Las Casas, whose death tolls are very high and cannot be verified.

hechos/fundacion-de-panama/resumen.texto: Pedrarias Dávila founded the city of Panama on August 15, 1519, next to a village of Indigenous fishermen on the Pacific coast, as the capital of Castilla del Oro. It became the base for expeditions to Nicaragua and Peru, the route for Peruvian silver to Nombre de Dios and Portobelo, and the seat of an audiencia from 1538. It was sacked and burned in 1671 during Henry Morgan’s attack, and rebuilt in 1673 on another site.

hechos/saqueo-de-portobelo-1668/titulo.texto: Sack of Portobelo by Henry Morgan

hechos/saqueo-de-portobelo-1668/resumen.texto: In July 1668 the privateer Henry Morgan, with about 500 men and a commission from the governor of Jamaica, took Portobelo by surprise, the port of the trade fairs with Peru. According to Exquemelin’s account, he used religious men and nuns as shields to storm a fort, and he tortured residents to reveal their goods; he collected a ransom of 100,000 pesos and withdrew.

hechos/saqueo-de-panama-1671/resumen.texto: At the end of 1670 Henry Morgan, with more than a thousand buccaneers, took the San Lorenzo castle at the mouth of the Chagres; in January 1671 he crossed the isthmus and defeated the Spanish militias in front of the city of Panama, which burned in a fire of disputed origin and was sacked for weeks. Because the action violated the 1670 peace treaty between Spain and England, Morgan was taken prisoner to London, though he was later knighted and named deputy governor of Jamaica.

hechos/colonia-escocesa-del-darien/resum.texto: The Company of Scotland, promoted by William Paterson, sent about 1,200 colonists in 1698 to found New Caledonia on the Caribbean coast of Darién, on lands Spain claimed and where the Guna lived, with whom they had good relations. Fevers, hunger and the lack of English support made it fail, and a second expedition capitulated to the Spanish in 1700; about 2,000 colonists died, and the bankruptcy weighed on the union of Scotland and England (1707).

hechos/pueblo-guna/resumen.texto: A Chibchan-speaking people of Darién and of the Caribbean coast of Panama and Colombia, organized in villages governed by congresses and chiefs (sailas). During the colonial period they resisted the Spaniards in Darién, traded, and sometimes allied with buccaneers, Scots and French; in the 19th century much of the population moved to the San Blas Islands.

hechos/revolucion-guna/resumen.texto: In February 1925 the Guna of the San Blas Islands, led by Nele Kantule and Simral Colman and with support from the American Richard Marsh, rose up against the Panamanian police who were repressing their customs. They killed police officers and Guna who supported the government, and proclaimed a Tule republic. An agreement reached with United States mediation ended the conflict and paved the way for the autonomous comarca recognized in 1938 and 1953.

hechos/nicaraos-y-chorotegas/resumen.texto: When the Spaniards arrived, the Pacific strip of Nicaragua and Nicoya was inhabited by Chorotegas (an Otomanguean-speaking people) and Nicaraos (a Nahuatl-speaking people), who had arrived from Mexico in the Postclassic period, in densely populated chiefdoms with markets, temples and cacao as money. Oviedo, who was there in 1527-1529, described their councils of elders, their trade, and also their wars, their slavery, their human sacrifices and the ritual consumption of captives’ flesh.

hechos/conquista-de-nicaragua/resumen.texto: In 1522-1523 Gil González Dávila traveled along the Pacific coast of Nicaragua, where he spoke with the cacique the chronicles call Nicarao and was attacked by the warriors of Diriangén. In 1524 Francisco Hernández de Córdoba, sent by Pedrarias, founded Granada and León; wars followed against Chorotegas, Nicaraos and other peoples, with Indigenous allies from Mexico, and disputes among conquistadors, until Pedrarias took over the government in 1527.

hechos/fundacion-de-granada-y-leon/resum.texto: Francisco Hernández de Córdoba founded Granada in 1524, beside Lake Cocibolca, and León, beside Lake Managua, in areas of dense Indigenous population. León was the capital of the province of Nicaragua until, after earthquakes and the activity of the Momotombo volcano, its residents abandoned it in 1610 and refounded it on its present site; its ruins, León Viejo, are a World Heritage Site.

hechos/trata-de-indios-de-nicaragua/titu.texto: Trade in Indigenous Slaves from Nicaragua

hechos/trata-de-indios-de-nicaragua/resu.texto: From 1526, governors and encomenderos of Nicaragua and Honduras branded as slaves Indigenous people taken in war or handed over by caciques as tribute, and shipped them to Panama and, from 1532, to Peru, where many died. The trade is documented in letters from bishops and royal officials, in Oviedo and Las Casas, and in the Crown’s prohibitions, which were enforced only with the New Laws and the presidency of Alonso López de Cerrato around 1550. Modern estimates of the number of people exported vary widely, from tens of thousands to nearly half a million, and Sherman, MacLeod and Newson consider it a central cause of the collapse of the population of the Nicaraguan Pacific.

hechos/pueblo-pipil/titulo.texto: The Pipil and the Lordship of Cuzcatlán

hechos/pueblo-pipil/resumen.texto: A Nahuatl-speaking people (Nahuat) of western and central El Salvador, who arrived from Mexico in Postclassic migrations and were organized in lordships such as Cuzcatlán and Izalco, with maize agriculture and large cacao production. After the conquest, Izalco’s cacao was the main wealth of the province in the 16th century; their language survives today with very few speakers.

hechos/conquista-de-cuzcatlan/resumen.texto: In June 1524 Pedro de Alvarado, with Nahua and Kaqchikel allies, entered Pipil territory and defeated them at Acajutla and Tacuzcalco, but did not manage to subdue them: they withdrew to the highlands and resisted. Gonzalo de Alvarado founded the villa of San Salvador in 1525, which was refounded in 1528 after new campaigns.

hechos/pueblo-lenca/resumen.texto: A people of the mountains of western and central Honduras and of eastern El Salvador, organized in lordships that allied with and fought against one another, with their own languages of disputed affiliation. They resisted the conquest in the 1537-1538 rebellion led by Lempira; afterward they were subjected to encomiendas and resettled into towns, and their languages were lost, although Lenca identity persists.

hechos/conquista-de-honduras/resumen.texto: Honduras was contested in 1524 by several expeditions: Gil González Dávila from the south and Cristóbal de Olid, sent by Cortés, who rebelled against him. Cortés himself arrived in 1525 after a march from Mexico during which he had Cuauhtémoc executed. Wars against the peoples of the interior, the slave trade and epidemics reduced the population; Francisco de Montejo and Alonso de Cáceres defeated Lempira’s rebellion, and Gracias a Dios (1536) and Comayagua (1537) were founded.

hechos/rebelion-de-lempira/resumen.texto: In 1537 the Lenca chief Lempira gathered peoples of western Honduras (according to Antonio de Herrera, some 30,000 warriors) and for months resisted, from the peñol of Cerquín, the forces of Francisco de Montejo and his Indigenous allies. Lempira died that year, treacherously during a negotiation according to Herrera or in combat according to a soldier’s probanza, and the uprising, which had spread to other areas of Honduras, was suppressed in 1538.

hechos/conquista-de-costa-rica/titulo.texto: Conquest of the Central Valley of Costa Rica

hechos/conquista-de-costa-rica/resumen.texto: After failed attempts from the 1520s onward, Juan de Cavallón entered the Central Valley of Costa Rica in 1561, and Juan Vázquez de Coronado completed the subjection of the Huetares and other chiefdoms between 1562 and 1564, largely through agreements with their leaders. Cartago was founded in 1563 as the capital of the province; the Talamanca region was never fully subjected.

hechos/rebelion-de-talamanca/resumen.texto: On September 29, 1709 the Bribri and Cabécar peoples of Talamanca, led by Pablo Presbere, rose against the Franciscan missionaries who were trying to resettle them: they killed two friars, soldiers and the wife of one of the friars, and burned fourteen churches. An expedition from Cartago captured Presbere and hundreds of Indigenous people, who were taken to the Central Valley; Presbere was executed by firing squad in Cartago in 1710, and Talamanca remained outside Spanish control.

hechos/reino-misquito/titulo.texto: The Miskito and the Kingdom of Mosquitia

hechos/reino-misquito/resumen.texto: The Miskito, a people of the Caribbean coast of Nicaragua and Honduras who incorporated Africans who arrived through shipwrecks and escapes (the “zambos misquitos”), allied from the 17th century with the English of Jamaica, who crowned their kings and supplied them with weapons. They attacked Spanish settlements and captured Indigenous people from other peoples to sell as slaves to the English. Great Britain kept a protectorate until 1860, and Nicaragua incorporated the region by force in 1894.

hechos/asentamiento-britanico-de-belice/.texto: From the mid-17th century British logwood and then mahogany cutters settled on the coast of Belize, on territory Spain claimed and where Maya peoples lived. The treaties of Paris (1763) and Versailles (1783) and the London convention (1786) recognized their right to cut timber without sovereignty; they depended on the labor of enslaved Africans, who were the majority of the population at the end of the 18th century. In 1798 they repelled a Spanish attack at St. George’s Caye, and in 1862 the settlement became the colony of British Honduras.

hechos/conquista-de-guatemala/resumen.texto: Pedro de Alvarado left Mexico at the end of 1523 with some 400 Spaniards and thousands of Nahua allies from Tlaxcala, Cholula, Mexico and other towns. In February 1524 he defeated the K’iche’ near Xelajú (Quetzaltenango), whose chief is remembered in the K’iche’ tradition as Tecún Umán (his historicity is disputed), and in March he burned the K’iche’ lords alive in Q’umarkaj. He allied with the Kaqchikels, enemies of the K’iche’ since they had separated from them around 1470, who rebelled in August 1524 over demands for gold and resisted until 1530, while the Mam, Tz’utujil, Poqomam and other peoples were subjected in campaigns in which Indigenous allies played a decisive role.

hechos/fundacion-de-santiago-de-guatemal.texto: Founding and Relocations of Santiago de Guatemala

Alvarado founded Santiago de los Caballeros de Guatemala on July 25, 1524, next to Iximché, the Kaqchikel capital; because of the rebellion of its former allies, the city moved in 1527 to the Almolonga valley (today Ciudad Vieja). It was destroyed in 1541 by a landslide from the Volcán de Agua, was refounded in 1543 in the Panchoy valley (today Antigua Guatemala), and after the earthquakes of 1773 the capital was moved in 1776 to the Valle de la Ermita, today Guatemala City.

hechos/destruccion-de-santiago-en-almolo.texto: Destruction of Santiago de Guatemala by the Volcán de Agua

On the night of September 10 to 11, 1541, after days of rain, an avalanche of water and mud came down from the Volcán de Agua and buried the city of Santiago, in Almolonga. The governor Beatriz de la Cueva, Alvarado’s widow, died, along with many Spanish and Indigenous residents; the account by the notary Juan Rodríguez, printed that year in Mexico by Juan Pablos, is considered the first news publication of the Americas.

hechos/verapaz/titulo.texto: Verapaz: The Project of Peaceful Conversion of Tezulutlán

hechos/verapaz/resumen.texto: In 1537 Bartolomé de las Casas and the Dominicans Pedro de Angulo and Luis de Cáncer agreed with the governor Alonso de Maldonado that the region of Tezulutlán, called the “land of war” for its resistance, would receive neither soldiers nor encomenderos if its towns peacefully accepted the friars. With the help of converted caciques, the region was incorporated without armed conquest and from 1547 was called Verapaz. The Dominican chronicler Remesal is the main source; other historians qualify the success because of the later forced concentration of towns and the wars against the Lacandones and Choles.

hechos/audiencia-de-guatemala/titulo.texto: Audiencia and Captaincy General of Guatemala

hechos/audiencia-de-guatemala/resumen.texto: A court and government created by the New Laws as the Audiencia de los Confines, installed in Gracias a Dios in 1544 and moved to Santiago de Guatemala in 1549. Its president, with the title of captain general, governed the Kingdom of Guatemala, from Chiapas to Costa Rica, under nominal dependence on the viceroy of New Spain. Under Alonso López de Cerrato (1548-1555) it freed thousands of enslaved Indigenous people and set new tribute rates.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-universidad-de-sa.texto: Founding of the University of San Carlos de Guatemala
University of San Carlos de Guatemala

Charles II founded the university by royal cédula of January 31, 1676, on the bequest that Bishop Francisco Marroquín had left for a college; it opened its courses in 1681 in Santiago de Guatemala, with chairs in theology, canon law, law, medicine and one Indigenous language. It was the first university in Central America and moved to Nueva Guatemala after the earthquakes of 1773.

hechos/rebelion-tzeltal-de-1712/resumen.texto: An uprising of about thirty Tzeltal, Tsotsil and Chol towns in the Altos de Chiapas, begun in Cancuc in August 1712 after the announcement of an apparition of the Virgin to the young María de la Candelaria. The rebels created their own Indigenous clergy, disavowed the Church and the king, and killed friars and Spanish residents; troops from Guatemala and Tabasco defeated them at the end of 1712, and the repression and famine that followed caused many deaths. Historians link it to the weight of tribute, the repartimientos of goods and ecclesiastical burdens.

hechos/terremotos-de-santa-marta/titulo.texto: Santa Marta Earthquakes and the Move of Guatemala's Capital

hechos/terremotos-de-santa-marta/resumen.texto: On July 29, 1773, Saint Martha's day, a series of earthquakes destroyed much of Santiago de Guatemala. After a long dispute between Captain General Martín de Mayorga, who favored the move, and Archbishop Pedro Cortés y Larraz, who opposed it, the Crown ordered the capital moved to the Ermita valley, where Nueva Guatemala de la Asunción was founded in 1776; the old city remained as Antigua Guatemala.

hechos/independencia-de-centroamerica/re.texto: On September 15, 1821, upon news of the Plan of Iguala and the independence of Chiapas, a junta of authorities and residents of Guatemala City declared independence from Spain, with Captain General Gabino Gaínza as political chief. In January 1822 most of the town councils approved annexation to the Mexican Empire, which San Salvador resisted and which Vicente Filísola's troops defeated; after Iturbide's fall, an assembly declared the absolute independence of the United Provinces of Central America on July 1, 1823. Panama became independent from Spain on November 28, 1821, and joined Gran Colombia.

hechos/republica-federal-de-centroameric.texto: Federation of Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua and Costa Rica organized by the Constitution of 1824; in April of that year its assembly abolished slavery, one of the first abolitions in the Americas. Wars between liberals and conservatives, with Francisco Morazán and Rafael Carrera as leaders, dissolved it between 1838 and 1841.

hechos/llegada-de-los-doce-franciscanos/.texto: Arrival of the Twelve Franciscans in Mexico

In 1524 twelve Franciscans led by Martín de Valencia arrived, among them Motolinía; according to the chronicles, Cortés received them on his knees before Indigenous lords. They began systematic evangelization: schools for sons of nobles, language learning, mass baptisms and the destruction of temples and images; the Dominicans (1526) and the Augustinians (1533) followed.

hechos/primera-audiencia-de-mexico/resum.texto: Tribunal and government presided over by Nuño de Guzmán, with the judges (oidores) Juan Ortiz de Matienzo and Diego Delgadillo, which governed New Spain between 1528 and 1530. Zumárraga and others denounced its abuses: branding and selling Indians as slaves, many of them sent to the Antilles from Pánuco, excessive tribute, and persecution of Cortés's supporters. The Crown replaced it with a second Audiencia (1531–1535), presided over by Sebastián Ramírez de Fuenleal, with Vasco de Quiroga as oidor.

hechos/escuela-de-san-jose-de-los-natura.texto: School of San José de los Naturales

Franciscan school founded by Pedro de Gante around 1527 next to the convent of San Francisco in Mexico City, where Indigenous children were taught reading, writing, singing, music and trades such as painting, carpentry and tailoring. Its open-air chapel gathered thousands of Indigenous worshippers, and its workshops trained the craftsmen of the religious works.

hechos/esclavitud-indigena-en-nueva-espa.texto: Enslavement of Indigenous People in New Spain

After the conquest, Spaniards branded as slaves Indigenous people taken in war and others bought as slaves “de rescate,” a form that already existed in Mesoamerica under other rules (the Nahua tlacotin). The Crown prohibited it in 1530, allowed it again in 1534 and abolished it with the New Laws (1542); around 1550 the Audiencia freed most Indigenous slaves, although the enslavement of captives continued in the northern frontier wars. Nuño de Guzmán sent thousands of slaves from Pánuco to the Antilles (1527–1529).

hechos/encomienda-y-repartimiento-en-nue.texto: Encomienda and Repartimiento of Labor in New Spain

From 1522 Cortés assigned towns in encomiendas, which gave Spaniards the tribute and labor of Indigenous people in exchange for protection and doctrine. The New Laws (1542) forbade granting new encomiendas and inheriting them, but in the face of resistance from encomenderos the Crown revoked the ban on inheritance in 1545; a cédula of 1549 prohibited personal service, and over time many encomiendas passed to the Crown.
