From the 1550s forced labor was organized by repartimiento: towns had to send, in rotation, a share of their men to public works, farming and mines in exchange for a wage set by the authorities. The agricultural repartimiento was abolished in 1633 and the mining one continued; the abuses are documented in complaints by the towns themselves, such as the Kingsborough Codex.

hechos/pueblos-hospital-de-santa-fe/resu.texto: Vasco de Quiroga founded with his own salary the pueblo-hospital of Santa Fe, next to Mexico City (1532), and that of Santa Fe de la Laguna, on the shore of Lake Pátzcuaro (1533), and promoted hospitals in many Purépecha towns. They gathered Indigenous families with common property, shift work, teaching of trades and a hospital for the sick and travelers. Quiroga defended them for decades in lawsuits with encomenderos and with the Audiencia.

hechos/fundacion-del-hospital-de-jesus/t.texto: Founding of the Hospital de Jesús

hechos/fundacion-del-hospital-de-jesus/r.texto: Hospital founded by Hernán Cortés around 1524 in Mexico City, next to the place where, according to tradition, he met Moctezuma in 1519. It treated poor patients, Cortés left it income in his will, and it still operates today, which is why it is considered the oldest hospital in the Americas in continuous use.

hechos/fundacion-de-puebla/titulo.texto: Founding of Puebla de los Ángeles

hechos/fundacion-de-puebla/resumen.texto: City founded in April 1531 by the second Audiencia and the Franciscans, with Motolinía present, as a town of Spaniards without encomiendas who would live from their own work, in a valley between Tlaxcala and Cholula; Indigenous workers from neighboring towns built it. It was the second city of New Spain, seat of a bishopric, of obrajes (textile workshops) and of talavera ware.

hechos/fundacion-del-colegio-de-tlatelol.texto: Founding of the College of Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco
College of Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco

Franciscan college opened on January 6, 1536, with support from Zumárraga and Viceroy Mendoza, for sons of the Indigenous nobility, who studied Latin, rhetoric, philosophy, music and medicine. Antonio Valeriano and the Nahua collaborators of Sahagún were trained there, and the Codex de la Cruz-Badiano was made, although some Spaniards opposed teaching Latin to Indians. From the 1570s, with epidemics, a lack of funds and the refusal to ordain Indigenous priests, it declined until it became a school for basic literacy.

hechos/proceso-de-don-carlos-ometochtzin.texto: Trial and Execution of Don Carlos Ometochtzin

Trial that Zumárraga, as apostolic inquisitor, conducted in 1539 against the lord of Texcoco, Don Carlos Ometochtzin, accused of keeping idols, living with a concubine and urging nobles to return to the old religion. He was burned in the main square of Mexico City on November 30, 1539. The punishment was criticized from Spain, and the case contributed to the Inquisition established in 1571 having no jurisdiction over Indians.

hechos/primera-imprenta-de-america/titul.texto: First Printing Press in the Americas

hechos/primera-imprenta-de-america/resum.texto: In 1539 the printer Juan Pablos, sent by the Sevillian Juan Cromberger at the request of Zumárraga and Viceroy Mendoza, set up the first documented printing press on the continent in the Casa de las Campanas in Mexico City. Until 1560 it printed at least 35 books, mainly doctrinal works, confessionals, grammars and vocabularies in Castilian, Nahuatl and other Indigenous languages; Lima had its first press only in 1584.

hechos/fundacion-del-colegio-de-san-nico.texto: Founding of the College of San Nicolás Obispo

College founded by Vasco de Quiroga in Pátzcuaro around 1540 to train priests who knew the Purépecha language; it moved to Valladolid (today Morelia) in 1580. Miguel Hidalgo was its student, professor and rector. It is the forerunner of the Universidad Michoacana de San Nicolás de Hidalgo.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-universidad-de-me.texto: Founding of the Royal University of Mexico
Royal and Pontifical University of Mexico

A royal cédula signed in the name of Charles V on September 21, 1551 created the University of Mexico with the privileges of Salamanca; it opened its courses in 1553 with Viceroy Luis de Velasco and in 1595 received the title of pontifical. It taught theology, canon law, law, medicine and the arts, and had a chair in Nahuatl. Noble Indigenous people could study there, but its students were mostly Creoles. It closed permanently in 1865.

hechos/hospital-real-de-naturales/titulo.texto: Founding of the Hospital Real de Naturales

hechos/hospital-real-de-naturales/resume.texto: Hospital for Indigenous people founded in Mexico City by a cédula of 1553 and opened with Viceroy Luis de Velasco, later financed by a contribution of half a real from Indigenous tributaries and by the income of a theater. It treated thousands of patients during the epidemics, and in 1576 Francisco Hernández and other physicians performed autopsies there on victims of the cocoliztli.

hechos/concilios-provinciales-mexicanos/.texto: Assemblies of the bishops of New Spain convened in 1555 and 1565 by Archbishop Montúfar and in 1585 by Pedro Moya de Contreras. The first forbade ordaining Indians, mestizos and mulattos as priests; the third, in force until the 19th century, regulated doctrine, sacraments and the use of Indigenous languages, condemned abuses against Indians and, when consulted by the viceroy, questioned the justice of the war of fire and blood against the Chichimecas.

hechos/congregaciones-de-indios/resumen.texto: Relocation of dispersed Indigenous populations into new towns laid out on a grid, with a church and a cabildo, in order to evangelize, collect tribute and organize labor. There were two major campaigns: around 1550–1564, driven by the friars and Viceroy Velasco, and between 1598 and 1607, after the epidemics, with congregation judges. Many families resisted or returned to their former settlements, and the lands left vacant often passed into Spanish hands.

hechos/republica-de-indios/resumen.texto: Legal order that separated Indigenous towns, the “república de indios,” from the “república de españoles”: the towns had their own cabildo with Indigenous governor, alcaldes and regidores, communal lands, community treasuries and special legal protection, and in exchange they paid tribute and provided labor. In theory Spaniards, Blacks and mestizos could not live in them; the cabildos left thousands of documents in Nahuatl, Mixtec, Maya and other languages. The separation was never fully achieved; mestizaje and haciendas eroded it, and the Constitution of Cádiz (1812) formally abolished it.

hechos/juzgado-general-de-indios/resumen.texto: Special court of New Spain for Indigenous lawsuits, with a brief, oral and free procedure for litigants, financed by the “medio real de ministros” paid by each tributary. It was organized between 1585 and 1607, mainly under Viceroy Luis de Velasco the younger, drawing on the custom of viceroys since Mendoza of hearing Indians' complaints in person, and it operated until 1820. Borah and Owensby show that Indigenous people used it on a massive scale, including against their own caciques and against other communities.

hechos/inquisicion-de-mexico/titulo.texto: Tribunal of the Inquisition in Mexico

hechos/inquisicion-de-mexico/resumen.texto: Tribunal of the Holy Office established in Mexico in 1571, with Pedro Moya de Contreras as its first inquisitor. By royal order Indians were placed outside its jurisdiction, and their religious offenses passed to the bishops. It pursued mainly bigamy, blasphemy, witchcraft, Judaizers and Protestants: at the auto de fe of 1574 it punished English sailors from Hawkins's fleet, and in 1596 and 1649 it burned Jewish converts such as Luis de Carvajal the Younger. One estimate speaks of around 50 executions over its whole history; it was abolished in 1820.

hechos/epidemias-de-cocoliztli/resumen.texto: Two major epidemics of a fever with hemorrhages, which the Nahuas called cocoliztli (“pestilence”), killed a large part of the Indigenous population of New Spain in 1545–1548 and 1576–1580, while Spaniards fell ill much less. Chroniclers give figures from hundreds of thousands to millions of deaths, and Acuña-Soto and colleagues (2002) estimate between 5 and 15 million in 1545, a figure that depends on how large the population is assumed to have been beforehand. The cause is debated: Acuña-Soto proposes a local hemorrhagic fever worsened by a severe drought, and ancient DNA from Teposcolula (Vågene and colleagues, 2018) identified Salmonella Paratyphi C, the cause of an enteric fever that may have come from Europe (it was found in Norway around the year 1200).

hechos/caida-de-la-poblacion-del-centro-.texto: Decline of the Indigenous Population of Central Mexico

The Indigenous population of central Mexico fell during the 16th century due to epidemics (smallpox in 1520, measles in 1531, cocoliztli in 1545 and 1576), wars, forced labor, famine and social disorganization, bottoming out around 1620. The figures are disputed: Cook and Borah calculated about 25 million for 1518 and a little over one million for 1605; Rosenblat proposed about 4.5 million for all of Mexico in 1492, and Zambardino (1980) between 5 and 10 million for the center in 1519. Most authors accept a drop of between two-thirds and nine-tenths, with epidemics as the main cause.

hechos/epidemia-de-matlazahuatl/resumen.texto: Epidemic of a fever that the Nahuas called matlazáhuatl, later identified with typhus or other fevers with no consensus, which killed tens of thousands of people in 1736–1739 in Mexico City and the center of the viceroyalty, mainly Indigenous people. In 1737 the city swore the Virgin of Guadalupe in as its patroness to stop it, a key step in the expansion of her cult.

hechos/esclavitud-africana-en-nueva-espa.texto: From the conquest on, enslaved Africans arrived in New Spain, mainly through Veracruz and in greater numbers between 1595 and 1640, under Portuguese asientos; Curtin (1969) estimated some 200,000 for the whole colony. They worked on sugar mills, obrajes, mines, estates and urban houses, and many fled or won their freedom. The palenque of Yanga, near Córdoba, resisted a Spanish expedition in 1609 and later obtained recognition as a free town, San Lorenzo de los Negros (between 1618 and 1641, depending on the sources). In 1612 the Audiencia had more than thirty Africans and mulattos accused of conspiring to rise up hanged in Mexico City. Around 1803 Humboldt counted only about 6,000 slaves, when most Afro-descendants were already free and mixed with other groups. Hidalgo decreed abolition in 1810, and a decree by Vicente Guerrero made it general in Mexico in 1829.

hechos/descubrimiento-de-la-plata-de-zac.texto: In September 1546 an expedition led by Juan de Tolosa, with Indigenous guides, found the silver veins of Zacatecas, which within a few years attracted Spanish miners, paid and forced Indigenous laborers and enslaved Africans. The boom opened the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro to the north and set off the Chichimeca War; Zacatecas was for decades the main mining center of New Spain.

hechos/guerra-chichimeca/resumen.texto: Half-century war between the Spaniards, with Otomí, Purépecha and Nahua allies, and the nomadic and semi-nomadic peoples collectively called Chichimecas (Guachichiles, Zacatecos, Guamares, Pames and others), triggered by the opening of the silver road to Zacatecas. The Chichimecas attacked convoys and estates, and the Spaniards responded with presidios, campaigns and the enslavement of captives, whose legitimacy theologians and the Third Mexican Council debated. It ended with the “peace by purchase” of Viceroys Villamanrique and Velasco the younger (1585–1600), which handed out food, clothing and land and settled Tlaxcalan colonists among the Chichimecas.

hechos/metodo-de-patio/resumen.texto: In 1554, in Pachuca, Bartolomé de Medina put into practice on a large scale the amalgamation of silver with mercury, salt and other reagents in open-air patios. The method made it possible to use poor ores and multiplied silver production in Mexico and, from the 1570s, in Peru. It depended on mercury from Almadén and Huancavelica and poisoned many workers.

hechos/galeon-de-manila/resumen.texto: Shipping line between Manila and Acapulco, opened in 1565 when Andrés de Urdaneta found the return route across the North Pacific. It carried American silver to Asia and brought back Chinese silks, porcelain and spices, as well as free and enslaved people from Asia. It linked America, Asia and Europe regularly for the first time. It operated until 1815.

hechos/tornaviaje-de-urdaneta/resumen.texto: Andrés de Urdaneta, pilot of Legazpi's expedition to the Philippines, left Cebu on June 1, 1565 and, sailing north to latitudes off Japan to take advantage of the westerly winds, reached Acapulco on October 8. It was the first planned return from Asia to America across the Pacific. Alonso de Arellano, who had separated from the fleet, had arrived earlier, in August, by a similar route.

hechos/rebelion-de-los-tepehuanes/resume.texto: Uprising of the Tepehuanes of Nueva Vizcaya (Durango), led by religious leaders who announced the expulsion of the Spaniards. It began in November 1616 with the killing of several Jesuit and Franciscan missionaries, settlers and Christian Indigenous people. The repression, with Indigenous allies, lasted until 1620, with many deaths on both sides and the enslavement of prisoners.

hechos/misiones-jesuitas-del-noroeste/ti.texto: Jesuit Missions of Northwestern New Spain

hechos/misiones-jesuitas-del-noroeste/re.texto: The Jesuits worked as missionaries from 1591 in Sinaloa and Sonora, from 1687 in Pimería Alta with Eusebio Kino, and from 1697 in Baja California with Juan María de Salvatierra (Loreto mission). The missions gathered semi-nomadic peoples into towns with a church, crops and livestock, under the authority of the fathers and presidio soldiers. There were rebellions (Pima in 1695 and 1751, Pericú in 1734), and epidemics greatly reduced the population of Baja California. After the expulsion of 1767 the missions passed to Franciscans and Dominicans.

hechos/culto-de-guadalupe/titulo.texto: The Cult of Guadalupe and the Debate over the Apparitions

hechos/culto-de-guadalupe/resumen.texto: According to tradition, the Virgin appeared in December 1531 to the Indigenous man Juan Diego on the Tepeyac hill and left her image on his tilma. Documents show a chapel with a venerated image from at least 1556, but the account of the apparitions was first printed in 1648 (Sánchez) and 1649 (Lasso de la Vega). García Icazbalceta (1883) and Poole (1995) maintain that it took shape in the 17th century, and defenders of its historicity invoke oral tradition, the Codex Escalada and the attribution of the Nican mopohua to Valeriano. Devotion grew with the epidemic of 1737, and in 1754 Pope Benedict XIV approved her patronage over New Spain.

hechos/desague-de-huehuetoca/titulo.texto: Huehuetoca Drainage and the Flood of 1629

hechos/desague-de-huehuetoca/resumen.texto: To protect Mexico City from the floods of its lakes, in 1607 Viceroy Luis de Velasco the younger commissioned Enrico Martínez to build a tunnel and canal through Huehuetoca toward the Tula River. Thousands of Indigenous workers under repartimiento dug it in a few months. The tunnel became blocked, and in September 1629 a flood began that kept the city under water until 1634, with many deaths and the emigration of part of the population. The work became an open cut, finished at the end of the 18th century.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-biblioteca-palafo.texto: On September 5, 1646, Bishop Juan de Palafox donated his nearly 5,000 books to the colleges of Puebla, on the condition that they be open to anyone who wanted to read them. It is considered the first public library in the Americas, and it preserves its 18th-century baroque hall with about 45,000 volumes.

hechos/motin-de-1692/resumen.texto: On June 8, 1692, amid a shortage of maize caused by rains and plagues, a crowd of Indians, mestizos, mulattos and poor Spaniards attacked and set fire to the viceregal palace and the cabildo houses. Carlos de Sigüenza y Góngora saved part of the archive and wrote an account very hostile to the Indians. The repression included executions, a temporary ban on pulque, and an order that Indigenous people return to live in their barrios, outside the Spanish city grid.

hechos/sociedad-de-castas/titulo.texto: The Caste Society and Casta Paintings

hechos/sociedad-de-castas/resumen.texto: In New Spain people were classified by their Spanish, Indigenous and African ancestry (mestizos, castizos, mulattos, moriscos and other “castas”), with effects on tribute, access to offices, guilds and religious orders, and marriage. In the 18th century dozens of series of “casta paintings” were produced, such as Miguel Cabrera's (1763), mainly for a European public. Historians agree that the categories were more flexible in practice than in the paintings: the records show changes of quality according to place, wealth and reputation.

hechos/rebelion-de-canek/resumen.texto: In November 1761, during a festival in Cisteil (Yucatán), the Maya Jacinto Uc de los Santos proclaimed himself king under the name Canek and called for the expulsion of the Spaniards. Militias took the town days later, with hundreds of Maya dead. Canek was executed in Mérida on December 14, other leaders were hanged, and dozens of prisoners were whipped and mutilated by having an ear cut off.

hechos/visita-de-galvez/titulo.texto: General Inspection of José de Gálvez

hechos/visita-de-galvez/resumen.texto: General inspection of New Spain commissioned by Charles III to José de Gálvez, who reorganized the treasury (tobacco monopoly, customs, alcabalas), carried out the expulsion of the Jesuits and the repression of 1767, and organized the occupation of Alta California (1769). As minister of the Indies (1776–1787) he extended his reforms: intendancies, the Comandancia de las Provincias Internas and free trade, which increased revenue and displaced Creoles from offices.

hechos/expulsion-de-los-jesuitas-de-nuev.texto: Expulsion of the Jesuits from New Spain and the Riots of 1767

On June 25, 1767, Charles III's order to expel the Jesuits was carried out in New Spain: hundreds of religious left for exile, among them Clavijero and Landívar, and their colleges, haciendas and missions passed to other orders or to the Crown. There were riots in San Luis Potosí, Guanajuato, Pátzcuaro and other cities, which the visitor José de Gálvez repressed. According to his own report, 85 people were hanged and hundreds sentenced to whipping, prison or exile.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-academia-de-san-c.texto: Founding of the Academy of San Carlos

First academy of fine arts in the Americas, born in 1781 from the engraving school of the Mint of Mexico, approved by Charles III in 1783 and inaugurated in 1785. It taught painting, sculpture, architecture and engraving according to neoclassicism, with professors such as Manuel Tolsá.

hechos/real-expedicion-botanica-a-nueva-.texto: Royal Botanical Expedition to New Spain

Scientific expedition of the Crown led by Martín Sessé, with José Mariano Mociño and the Mexican illustrators Atanasio Echeverría and Juan de Dios Vicente de la Cerda, which traveled through New Spain, the Antilles, Central America and the Pacific coast as far as Nootka. It created the Botanical Garden and the chair of botany in Mexico, and gathered thousands of descriptions and illustrations of plants, which remained unpublished until the late 19th century.

hechos/censo-de-revillagigedo/resumen.texto: First general census of New Spain, ordered by the viceroy, the Count of Revillagigedo, which counted the population by intendancy with data on caste (Spanish, Indian, mestizo, mulatto), occupation and age, although some provinces remained incomplete. Humboldt used it to estimate in 1803 some 5.8 million inhabitants, of whom about 2.5 million were Indigenous.

hechos/fundacion-del-real-seminario-de-m.texto: Founding of the Royal Seminary of Mining

Technical school created by the Royal Mining Tribunal and opened on January 1, 1792 under the direction of Fausto de Elhuyar, with chairs in mathematics, physics, chemistry and mineralogy. Andrés Manuel del Río taught there, and Humboldt praised it in 1803. Its seat, the Palacio de Minería designed by Manuel Tolsá, was built between 1797 and 1813.

hechos/descubrimiento-del-vanadio/resume.texto: In 1801 Andrés Manuel del Río, a professor at the Seminario de Minería, found a new element in a lead ore from Zimapán, which he called erythronium. An analysis by the French chemist Collet-Descotils mistakenly attributed it to chromium, and Del Río withdrew his finding. Nils Sefström rediscovered it in 1830 as vanadium, and Del Río's priority was later recognized.

hechos/real-expedicion-filantropica-de-l.texto: Royal Philanthropic Expedition of the Vaccine

Expedition financed by the Crown and led by Francisco Javier de Balmis, which left A Coruña on November 30, 1803 with 22 foundlings and the matron Isabel Zendal, to carry the smallpox vaccine alive by passing it arm to arm. It vaccinated in Puerto Rico, Venezuela, Cuba and New Spain, where vaccine boards were created. In 1805 it went on to the Philippines with 26 Mexican children, reaching Macao and Canton; its South American branch, under José Salvany, reached as far as Peru and Charcas. It is estimated to have vaccinated hundreds of thousands of people.

hechos/consolidacion-de-vales-reales/res.texto: Royal cédula of 1804 that required the ecclesiastical institutions of New Spain to hand over to the Crown the capital they had lent to landowners, merchants and miners, to pay Spain's war debt. Debtors had to repay the loans all at once or lose their property. The measure hit mainly middling Creole property owners, was denounced by the bishop-elect Manuel Abad y Queipo, and fed discontent before 1808. It was suspended in 1808.

hechos/crisis-de-1808-en-mexico/resumen.texto: When the Bayonne abdications became known, the Creole city council of Mexico City, with Francisco Primo de Verdad and Fray Melchor de Talamantes, proposed a junta to govern in the king's name, and Viceroy José de Iturrigaray seemed to accept it. On September 15, 1808, Peninsular merchants led by Gabriel de Yermo deposed him by force, and Primo de Verdad and Talamantes died in prison. The coup closed the legal path and opened the way to the conspiracies of Valladolid (1809) and Querétaro (1810).

hechos/toma-de-la-alhondiga-de-granadita.texto: Capture of the Alhóndiga de Granaditas

On September 28, 1810, Hidalgo's insurgent crowd, made up mainly of Indigenous people and mine and hacienda workers, took the granary of Guanajuato, where the intendant Juan Antonio Riaño had taken refuge with soldiers and Spanish and Creole families. Riaño, the defenders and numerous civilians died, and the city was sacked; Allende reproached Hidalgo for these excesses. When Calleja retook the city in November he ordered reprisal executions, and from 1811 the heads of Hidalgo, Allende, Aldama and Jiménez hung from the corners of the Alhóndiga until 1821.

hechos/batalla-de-puente-de-calderon/res.texto: On January 17, 1811, near Guadalajara, the royalist army of Félix Calleja, of about 6,000 men, defeated the forces of Hidalgo and Allende, tens of thousands of people, mostly poorly armed. The insurgent leaders fled north and were captured at Acatita de Baján in March.

hechos/ejecucion-de-hidalgo/titulo.texto: Trial and Execution of Miguel Hidalgo

hechos/ejecucion-de-hidalgo/resumen.texto: Captured in March 1811, Hidalgo was tried in Chihuahua by a military court and stripped of his orders by the ecclesiastical authority. In his statements he acknowledged having ordered the deaths of hundreds of Spanish prisoners in Valladolid and Guadalajara. He was shot on July 30, 1811, after Allende, Aldama and Jiménez.

hechos/congreso-de-chilpancingo/resumen.texto: Insurgent congress convened by Morelos in Chilpancingo on September 13, 1813, which named him generalísimo and declared independence on November 6. Pursued by the royalists, it sanctioned the Constitution of 1814 in Apatzingán. It was the first attempt to give the insurgency a representative government.

hechos/ejecucion-de-morelos/resumen.texto: Captured at Temalaca in November 1815 while protecting the congress's retreat, Morelos was tried by the ecclesiastical jurisdiction and the Inquisition, which declared him a heretic and degraded him, and by a military court. He was shot in San Cristóbal Ecatepec on December 22, 1815.

hechos/independencia-de-mexico/resumen.texto: War begun with Hidalgo's uprising in September 1810 and continued by Morelos, Guerrero and other insurgent leaders against the royalist army, with violence on both sides. After years of guerrilla warfare, the royalist officer Agustín de Iturbide allied with Guerrero in the Plan of Iguala (1821), won over almost the entire army and entered Mexico City with the Army of the Three Guarantees on September 27, 1821. The next day the act of independence of the Mexican Empire was signed. Spain recognized it in 1836.

hechos/primer-imperio-mexicano/resumen.texto: Constitutional monarchy born from independence, with Iturbide as regent and, from May 1822, as Emperor Agustín I. In January 1822 the former kingdom of Guatemala was annexed to it. At odds with the congress, which he dissolved, and with the Plan of Casa Mata, Iturbide abdicated in March 1823. Mexico was organized as a federal republic (1824), and Central America, except Chiapas, separated.

hechos/virreinato-de-nueva-espana/resume.texto: Kingdom of the Spanish monarchy created in 1535 and governed by a viceroy from Mexico City, which stretched from today's southern United States to Central America, with its own audiencia, and on which the Antilles and the Philippines depended. It was organized into audiencias, governorates, alcaldías mayores and, from 1786, intendancies. It was the richest and most populous kingdom of the Indies, sustained by silver. It lasted until independence in 1821.

lugares/ciudad-de-mexico/resumen.texto: Capital of New Spain, built from 1522 on the ruins of Tenochtitlan with forced Indigenous labor, with a Spanish grid in the center and Indigenous parcialidades (San Juan Tenochtitlan and Santiago Tlatelolco) with their own government. It was the largest city in the Americas during the colonial period, seat of the viceroy, the audiencia, the archbishopric, the university, the printing press and the Inquisition. It is the capital of independent Mexico.

lugares/hospital-de-jesus/resumen.texto: Hospital founded by Hernán Cortés around 1524 in Mexico City, which still operates and is considered the oldest hospital in the Americas in continuous use. Cortés's remains rest in its church.

lugares/colegio-de-santa-cruz-de-tlatelo.texto: College of Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco

Franciscan college of higher education for sons of the Indigenous nobility, opened in 1536 next to the convent of Santiago Tlatelolco. Latin, rhetoric, philosophy and medicine were taught there, the Florentine Codex and the Codex de la Cruz-Badiano were made, and Nahua governors and notaries were trained.

lugares/colegio-de-san-nicolas/resumen.texto: College founded by Vasco de Quiroga in Pátzcuaro around 1540 and moved to Valladolid (Morelia) in 1580, where Miguel Hidalgo studied and served as rector. It is the forerunner of the Universidad Michoacana.

lugares/real-universidad-de-mexico/nombr.texto: Royal and Pontifical University of Mexico

lugares/real-universidad-de-mexico/resum.texto: University created by royal cédula of 1551 and opened in 1553, with the privileges of Salamanca and a pontifical title since 1595. It trained the lawyers, physicians and clergy of the viceroyalty for almost three centuries and closed permanently in 1865.

lugares/puebla/resumen.texto: City founded in 1531 as a town of Spaniards without encomiendas, the second city of the viceroyalty, seat of a bishopric, of obrajes and of talavera ware. It preserves the Biblioteca Palafoxiana and a 17th-century cathedral.

lugares/patzcuaro/resumen.texto: Ancient Purépecha center beside the lake of the same name, which Vasco de Quiroga chose as seat of the bishopric of Michoacán and of his College of San Nicolás. It preserves the memory of “Tata Vasco” and the crafts attributed to his encouragement.

lugares/santa-fe-de-la-laguna/resumen.texto: Purépecha town on the shore of Lake Pátzcuaro, founded by Vasco de Quiroga as a pueblo-hospital in 1533. It preserves its hospital, its chapel and the memory of its communal ordinances.

lugares/zacatecas/resumen.texto: Mining town that arose after the silver discovery of 1546, which for decades was the main producing center of New Spain and the gateway to the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro. Its historic center is a World Heritage Site.

lugares/guanajuato/resumen.texto: Mining town that arose after the silver discovery around 1548. With the La Valenciana mine, from the 1760s, it was one of the world's largest silver producers at the end of the 18th century. The taking of the Alhóndiga de Granaditas took place there in 1810.

lugares/acapulco/resumen.texto: Pacific port and American terminus of the Manila galleon from 1565, defended by the Fort of San Diego. The galleon's annual arrival gave rise to a large merchants' fair.

lugares/san-juan-de-ulua/resumen.texto: Fortress on an islet off Veracruz, where in 1568 the Spanish fleet surprised John Hawkins and Francis Drake. It was the last Spanish stronghold in Mexico until its surrender in November 1825, and afterward it served as a prison.

lugares/catedral-metropolitana-de-mexico.texto: Cathedral built between 1573 and 1813 on the sacred precinct of ancient Tenochtitlan, next to the ruins of the Templo Mayor. It is one of the largest in the Americas and combines styles from the Renaissance to neoclassicism.

lugares/basilica-de-guadalupe/resumen.texto: Shrine at the foot of the Tepeyac hill, north of Mexico City, where the image of the Virgin of Guadalupe has been venerated since at least the 1550s. The basilica of 1709 and the modern one of 1976 made it one of the most visited Catholic shrines in the world.

lugares/biblioteca-palafoxiana/resumen.texto: Library in Puebla formed in 1646 with the donation of Bishop Juan de Palafox, open to any reader, and considered the first public library in the Americas. Its baroque hall holds about 45,000 volumes.

lugares/palacio-de-mineria/resumen.texto: Neoclassical building by Manuel Tolsá, built between 1797 and 1813 for the Royal Mining Seminary of Mexico, the first technical mining school in the Americas, where Fausto de Elhuyar and Andrés Manuel del Río taught.

lugares/alhondiga-de-granaditas/resumen.texto: Granary of Guanajuato built between 1798 and 1809, scene of the massacre of September 28, 1810 and, between 1811 and 1821, of the display of the heads of Hidalgo, Allende, Aldama and Jiménez.

lugares/antigua-guatemala/resumen.texto: Third seat of Santiago de Guatemala, capital of the kingdom from 1543 to 1776, with the University of San Carlos, convents and hospitals. The earthquakes of 1773 led to the move of the capital. It is a World Heritage Site.

lugares/guatemala-ciudad/resumen.texto: Nueva Guatemala de la Asunción, founded in 1776 in the Ermita valley as the fourth seat of the kingdom's capital after the earthquakes of 1773. The act of independence of 1821 was signed there, and it was the capital of the Federal Republic of Central America.

lugares/universidad-de-san-carlos-de-gua.texto: University of San Carlos de Guatemala
First university in Central America, created in 1676 and opened in 1681 in Santiago de Guatemala, on the bequest of Bishop Marroquín. It moved to Nueva Guatemala after the earthquakes of 1773.

lugares/san-salvador/resumen.texto: Town founded in 1525 by Gonzalo de Alvarado in Pipil land and refounded in 1528. It was the seat of the alcaldía mayor and later the intendancy of San Salvador, a center of indigo, and it is the capital of El Salvador.

lugares/comayagua/resumen.texto: City founded in 1537 in the central valley of Honduras, capital of the province of Honduras and seat of the bishopric during the colonial period.

lugares/leon-viejo/resumen.texto: Ruins of the first city of León, founded in 1524 by Francisco Hernández de Córdoba and abandoned in 1610 after earthquakes and the activity of the Momotombo volcano. It is a World Heritage Site, and remains attributed to Hernández de Córdoba and to Pedrarias Dávila have been identified there.

lugares/granada-nicaragua/resumen.texto: City founded in 1524 beside Lake Cocibolca, the port of departure toward the Caribbean by way of the San Juan River. It was sacked by buccaneers in the 17th century and set on fire by the filibuster William Walker in 1856.

lugares/leon-nicaragua/resumen.texto: City refounded in 1610 after the abandonment of León Viejo, capital of the province of Nicaragua, seat of the bishopric and of a seminary that gave rise to a university at the beginning of the 19th century.

lugares/cartago-costa-rica/resumen.texto: City founded in 1563 by Juan Vázquez de Coronado, capital of the province of Costa Rica throughout the colonial period.

lugares/ciudad-de-belice/resumen.texto: Settlement of British cutters of logwood and mahogany at the mouth of the Belize River, center of the colony of British Honduras.

lugares/panama-viejo/resumen.texto: Ruins of the first city of Panama, founded in 1519 by Pedrarias Dávila on the Pacific coast and destroyed in 1671 during the attack of Henry Morgan. It is a World Heritage Site.

lugares/portobelo/resumen.texto: Port founded in 1597 on the Caribbean coast of Panama, which replaced Nombre de Dios as the seat of the galleon fairs with Peru. It was attacked by William Parker (1601), Henry Morgan (1668) and Edward Vernon (1739), and its fortifications are a World Heritage Site.

lugares/santa-maria-la-antigua-del-darie.texto: Santa María la Antigua del Darién
Ruins of the first stable Spanish city on the mainland, founded in 1510 by Enciso and Balboa in Darién and abandoned in 1524. It was the seat of the first bishopric on the continent.

lugares/guayabo/resumen.texto: Indigenous settlement on the slopes of the Turrialba volcano, occupied from around 1000 BC to around AD 1400, with stone mounds, paved causeways, aqueducts and tanks. It is Costa Rica's main archaeological site.

lugares/esferas-de-piedra-del-diquis/res.texto: More than 300 stone spheres carved by the chiefdoms of the Diquís delta, in southern Costa Rica, between the 4th and 16th centuries, placed in alignments in front of the houses of the chiefs. Their exact meaning is unknown. Four of these settlements have been World Heritage Sites since 2014.
